news.title: Ousted Katie Zacharia Shares Halloween Guide to Dressing Up as Her
news.text: President Donald Trump's shortest-serving press secretary is offering unexpected inspiration for Halloween costume hunters, circulating the details of her go-to outfit during her week in the White House. "Fit Check for Halloween Fans: Veronica Beard Blazer and Skirt: Size 00, even after four kids. Christian Louboutin Miss Z in lamb nappa leather, 100 mm stiletto (sold out). Blouse: Nordstrom (sold out). Good luck!" Katie Zacharia posted on X Friday. In an interview earlier this week with Newsmax's Rob Finnerty, she encouraged people to dress up as her for Halloween. (Although the outfit retails at roughly $2,500.) "I hope you do dress up as me because it's absolutely hilarious. We will be dressing up as a family. I will wear the OG costume and stay tuned to what my kids will be," she said. Newsweek reached out to Zacharia for comment. Who Is Katie Zacharia? The conservative commentator previously worked as the communications adviser for Trump’s Truth Social platform and for the Department of Homeland Security. She earned her law degree from Pepperdine Caruso School of Law in 2011, but failed the bar exam, a disclosure that became a point of contention during her week at the White House. She is married and lives with her four children in Southern California. Trump fired Zacharia on October 16 after just five days as White House press secretary, saying that she had been treated “very badly” by the media. “I told Katie that in my opinion she was treated very, very unfairly by the news. Let’s call it the fake news,” Trump said. “I want her to have a good life. She’s being brutalized by the media.” Halloween Economics If you were to replicate Zacharia's stated outfit for Halloween, the $2,500 costume is roughly 67 times the amount the average American spends on a costume, according to National Retail Federation survey data showing typical costume spending of about $37 per person, one of the few things that haven't risen in cost dramatically over the past few years. But while Halloween costume costs have remained relatively stable, Halloween candy prices have jumped roughly 78 percent since 2020, making candy one of the fastest-rising Halloween expenses. The culprits are cocoa and sugar. Extreme climate conditions in West Africa affected cocoa production. Similarly, droughts in Mexico have affected sugar production. Regardless of the reason, a LendingTree survey said about 35 percent of consumers planned to skip buying Halloween candy altogether this year because of it. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Katie Zacharia shares the exact outfit you need to dress like her for Halloween.
news.author: Jennifer Radcliffe

news.title: US Scraps Traditional G20 Photo As Europeans Object To Posing With Russia's Lavrov
news.text: The top diplomats from the Group of 20 largest world economies opened two days of meetings in Atlanta on Friday after European objections to Russia's participation forced the US to cancel a photo of the foreign ministers, underscoring deep rifts among the group over global crises.Secretary of State Marco Rubio pulled the plug on the traditional group photo after several European officials threatened to boycott or walk out of the snapshot that usually helps kick off such diplomatic gatherings. But he still opened the talks, which otherwise went ahead as planned, with an appeal for unity on the issues that threaten international security and trade."We are in a critical moment - I would call it a moment of choosing, and I would say not just for my country, the United States of America, but frankly, for the world," Rubio told his colleagues."We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises," he added, pointing to disruptions to global energy and food supplies, trade and freedom of navigation. Many are posing "severe threats to essential foundations of the global economic order."Yet there was no sign that the G20 diplomats could come to consensus on many of the most contentious issues they face. Among them are the Russia-Ukraine conflict, the US-Israeli war against Iran, US tariffs and Chinese machinations in the South China Sea. All have contributed to spikes in the global cost of fuel as well as trade uncertainty.Concerns about any prospects for the talks escalated when the Europeans baulked at being photographed with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. Rubio decided to scrap the picture because he thought the controversy would be a distraction, according to two US officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter.Some G20 countries had already expressed concern that the U.S. invited Russia during its heightened attacks on Ukraine, especially after Trump pushed ties with Ukraine to new lows by waiving fresh sanctions on Moscow and temporarily limiting logistical and intelligence assistance.The British Foreign Office said in a statement that the United Kingdom "has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since the invasion of Ukraine and we are not about to change that."Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski said the cancellation of the group photo was "the right decision" by the U.S., telling media in Atlanta that "I am not the only one who does not want to be photographed with Lavrov."German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said "there is no normality with Russia" but "we must exchange the controversies at the table here," the German news agency dpa reported. He added that "we also must not send falsely optimistic signals."Lavrov has travelled only infrequently to NATO member states since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022 and resulting severe sanctions were imposed on Moscow. His presence in Atlanta could cause domestic political problems for Trump just days before the US congressional midterm elections as well as roil the G20, according to Ian Kelly, a US ambassador to Georgia during Trump's first term."It seems politically boneheaded to invite him," said Kelly, who now teaches international relations and diplomacy at Northwestern University outside Chicago.The meeting in Atlanta is meant to set the stage for a G20 leaders' summit hosted by President Donald Trump at his Miami golf club in December. It is unclear if Russian President Vladimir Putin will accept Trump's invitation to that gathering.Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous such meetings, was not invited this year as US officials said they made a conscious choice to include only formal members of the group.But missing from the invite list was South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group. South Africa is embroiled in several bitter disputes with the Trump administration, and when it chaired the G20 last year, top US officials, including Trump and Rubio, shunned the meetings it hosted."We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary," said Phindile Kunene, spokesperson for South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola.Kunene welcomed support from other G20 members that had expressed reservations about the exclusion and said South Africa was ready to participate "on an equal footing with other members" when Britain takes over the presidency next year.The US has said a top priority for the meeting is resolving differences over issues related to freedom of navigation, particularly in the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, the Black Sea and the South China Sea. The topic will include discussions on Iran, Russia-Ukraine and China and its smaller neighbours.But hanging over the meeting is the prospect of new US military intervention in Iran, which has put the region, including G20 member Saudi Arabia, on edge.The Associated Press has reported that US officials have told several Middle East countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military strikes against Iran after Tuesday's midterm elections and the possibility that Iran will retaliate against them.(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)
news.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio pulled the plug on the traditional group photo after several European officials threatened to boycott or walk out of the snapshot that usually helps kick off such diplomatic gatherings.
news.author: Prapti Upadhayay

news.title: Flavio Bolsonaro says in livestream he left Brazil due to 'persecution'
news.text:
Former Brazilian conservative presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro says he fled to the United States because he was a victim of "persecution" in his country.

Mr Bolsonaro, who lost Sunday's election runoff to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, secretly left Brazil on Tuesday and arrived in Florida aboard a private jet on Wednesday, after travelling through Argentina and Ecuador.

"The persecution began even sooner than I imagined," the senator said during an Instagram livestream in which he discussed his decision to flee after his Brazilian passports were cancelled as part of a money-laundering investigation.

In the video, first posted on X by right-wing influencer Simon Levy, Mr Bolsonaro recounted how police informed him on Monday that his passports were being revoked.

It came after a visit to his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is under house arrest.

"With tears in his eyes, he told me, 'You know where they're going with this, don't you?'" he said of his father.

"I told him, 'Dad, I know … Now I know what I have to do.'"

Although he gave no details of how he left the country, he said he and his wife made the decision "without anyone knowing" and urged people not to "point the finger at anyone".

US President Donald Trump and Argentine President Javier Milei are under pressure to explain the involvement of the US and Argentina in the senator's escape.

"I didn't leave Brazil, I left for Brazil," Flavio Bolsonaro said, alleging that Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes had made false accusations against him.

He also suggested there had been irregularities in the runoff, comparing them to "handball goals" that were not disallowed by VAR, without detailing what those irregularities might have been.

He also predicted that the economy would "go bust" under Mr Lula and said he was willing to run for president again.

"I'm not talking about 2030, I'm talking about before then," Mr Bolsonaro said.

The Trump administration does not plan to back Mr Bolsonaro's claim to be Brazil's rightful leader, according to a US official and another person familiar with the matter

Mr Trump had said Brazil's election on Sunday looked "rigged" but has pointed out that he offered no endorsement in the hotly contested race.

He also said he gets along well with 81-year-old Mr Lula, who beat the odds to clinch re-election by 3.5 percentage points.

The Bolsonaro departure was the latest chapter in a tumultuous period in Brazilian politics and in US-Brazil relations.

Bolsonaro's father was president from 2019 to 2023, then lost re-election to Mr Lula and was jailed last year for his self-coup attempt. 

Mr Lula himself spent 17 months in jail in 2018 and 2019 on corruption charges that were later annulled.

The US last year slapped sanctions on the judge overseeing the trial of the elder Bolsonaro and other Brazilian officials. 

Washington lifted the sanctions after Mr Trump and Mr Lula had a notably cordial interaction at the UN General Assembly.

During the campaign, Brazil objected to what it called attempts by some US officials to boost the Bolsonaro campaign, and the government has refused to seat the incoming US ambassador to Brazil, a close ally of Secretary of State Marco Rubio, in part due to those objections.
news.summary: In an Instagram livestream, the defeated Brazilian conservative presidential candidate says he and his wife fled to the United States "without anyone knowing".
news.author: ABC News

news.title: Haley Stevens Could Be Paving Way for Rogers Endorsement: Ex-Obama Adviser
news.text: Former Obama adviser David Axelrod suggested that Democratic Representative Haley Stevens could be paving the way for an endorsement of Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers, as she and Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed clashed days before a planned joint campaign appearance in Michigan. “It feels like she's almost setting up an endorsement of Rogers,” Axelrod said Friday night during an appearance on CNN's Anderson Cooper 360. Stevens had announced plans to appear alongside El-Sayed and South Carolina Representative Jim Clyburn at a Detroit church Sunday, marking the first time in months the two Democrats were expected to appear together. However, it remains unclear whether the event will go ahead following their latest exchange. In a statement Friday, Stevens called on El-Sayed to formally condemn a Rebellion PAC ad that linked U.S. support for Israel to rising grocery prices. She also called on him to apologize for his own comments linking Israel to the state's affordability challenges and urged him to take down his campaign ad featuring Tucker Carlson. “Abdul promises to get money out of politics. He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford,” Stevens said in a lengthy statement shared on X. The Rebellion PAC ad suggested that U.S. support for Israel was contributing to rising costs for American families. Stevens characterized the ad as antisemitic and said El-Sayed needed to publicly reject it. Rogers praised Stevens late Friday, calling her a “courageous leader” who deserved “the respect of every Michigan voter.” “She was absolutely right to call on Abdul El-Sayed to denounce the Rebellion PAC ad and she was right to call on him to apologize for espousing the same hateful ideology behind it,” Rogers posted on X. El-Sayed pushed back, accusing Stevens of seeming “intent on relitigating a primary" that ended three months ago. “Our campaign is and has always been focused on addressing the most critical challenges Michiganders are facing: Skyrocketing gas prices, unaffordable groceries, and the inability to see a doctor,” he said. El-Sayed campaign spokesperson Roxie Richner previously told Newsweek that the ad was “not affiliated in any way” with the Abdul for Senate campaign. Newsweek reached out to El-Sayed and Stevens for comment late Friday night. Axelrod pointed to Stevens' comments over the past few days, saying they seemed “aimed at trying to undermine” El-Sayed's campaign. “Maybe she's never gotten over the fact that she lost the primary,” Axelrod said. He called the ad offensive, saying El-Sayed should have rejected it but did not need to respond to Stevens' latest comments. The former rivals have largely kept their distance since Stevens narrowly lost the August primary to El-Sayed. But Stevens said Wednesday that she planned to vote for him, despite her fiancé's public endorsement of Rogers. Weeks of efforts to rally Democrats behind El-Sayed followed his narrow victory over Stevens, who drew significant support from Jewish and Black voters, fueling concerns over turnout among those blocs in the general election. Conservative commentator Scott Jennings said during an interview on CNN that he expected a record number of Michigan voters to back Republicans, arguing that El-Sayed's refusal to denounce the ad could hurt Democrats. “Haley Stevens is trying to drag her party away from the vile anti-Semitism that has defined the El Sayed campaign. And he’s sent a clear message—no thanks,” Jennings posted on X. CNN political commentator Van Jones said something was going “horribly wrong” in Michigan’s Senate race, criticizing Republicans for “anti-Muslim fear-mongering” and two Democratic-aligned ads for trafficking in “hate and intolerance” and alarming Black and Jewish voters. “That ad — and Abdul’s refusal to forthrightly denounce it — is scaring some Jewish Democrats in Michigan, who now are more reluctant to vote for him,” Jones wrote on X. President Donald Trump also weighed in on the contested race Friday night during a rally in Daytona Beach, Florida, saying El-Sayed did not like Jewish or Black people. “[El-Sayed] doesn't like Jewish people and he doesn't like Black people,” Trump said. However, while on the campaign trail, El-Sayed has visited several Black congregations. Along the way, he held a town hall at the Shrine of the Black Madonna to acknowledge the "tensions" between Black and Arab Americans, the Religion News Service reported. While there, he borrowed from Martin Luther King Jr.’s “I Have a Dream” speech, saying, “I also ask that I am judged by the content of my character, not the color of my skin,” he said at the September 14 event, drawing applause. RealClearPolitics rates the Michigan U.S. Senate race as a toss-up, with its polling average showing El-Sayed leading Rogers 49.2 percent to 45.6 percent, a 3.6-point advantage, as of Thursday. More than 1.42 million Michigan voters had cast their ballots as of Friday, according to the Michigan Secretary of State. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Stevens and El-Sayed clashed days before a planned joint campaign appearance in Michigan.
news.author: Alex Backus

news.title: Canada, EU launch new alliance with deals on Ukraine, minerals, AI
news.text:
MONTREAL: The EU and Canada announced an alliance on Friday aimed at cementing their own relations in the face of President Donald Trump’s moves to tear up US ties with its old partners.

After a two-day summit in Montreal, the EU said Canada will join a 90 billion euro ($103bn) support loan for Ukraine and work closely with Brussels on anything from critical minerals to artificial intelligence.

“The world’s becoming more dangerous and divided. Our societies are being shaken by new storms,” Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney told a press conference, mentioning eroding democratic norms and “the weaponisation of trade”.

“Together, Canada and the European Union are anchoring the ground. Anchoring our ground to uphold our values while forming a protective canopy under which our citizens can all thrive,” he said after talks with EU chiefs Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa.

Already sharing a free trade agreement, Canada and the EU have sought to move closer together since Trump’s shock return to power.

Both Canada and the EU have been hit with US tariffs and territorial threats. Ahead of the talks on Friday, Von der Leyen, the European Commission’s president, said Canada could not become a “full-fledged” EU member due to its geographical location, but the bloc wanted to bring it “as close as possible”.

Carney said Canada will join the EU’s 90bn euro support loan for Ukraine with an initial participation of 500 million euros.

The announcement comes at a time when Brussels is looking for help to plug gaps in Kyiv’s finances.

news.title: Judge orders Trump administration to cease threats to prosecute election officials
news.text:
WASHINGTON: A US judge ordered ​the Justice Department on Friday to stop threatening to prosecute state and local election officials who do not comply with the Trump administration’s demands related to voting by alleged non-citizens.

The ruling comes days before next week’s US midterm elections that will determine control of Congress, where Republicans currently hold narrow majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate. Although several key races appear closely contested, polls favor Democrats ‌to take control ‌of the House and give them a ​plausible ‌chance ⁠of ​a Senate ⁠majority.

In the months leading up to the midterms, President Donald Trump’s administration has taken an aggressive approach to election oversight, such as pressing states for voter-registration data, saying stricter measures are needed to ensure election security and public confidence in the vote.

But the Justice Department went too far this month when it threatened to prosecute state and ⁠county officials who do not cooperate with the Trump ‌administration’s election-related initiatives, US District Judge ‌Trina Thompson ruled in connection with a lawsuit ​brought by election workers’ unions and ‌some other groups.

“Because the public has a paramount interest ‌in ensuring that election officials and workers are able to carry out their work in accordance with federal law and election procedure, and the official day of the Elections is only a couple of days away, the balance of ‌the equities and public interest weigh in Plaintiffs’ favor,” Thompson wrote in her temporary restraining order.

The Justice ⁠Department had ⁠no immediate comment on the ruling.

Critics, including political experts as well as Democratic and some Republican election officials, have viewed the Trump administration’s moves as federal overreach. Some election officials have told Reuters they were preparing for potential federal interference in the midterm elections.

Thompson, who was appointed by former President Joe Biden, ordered the Trump administration to refrain from demanding that local election officials remove voters from statewide rolls, refuse ballots to specific voters, or segregate ballots cast in the midterm elections, based on a Trump administration list of alleged ​non-citizen voters.

Trump has made false ​claims related to elections in the past, including not acknowledging his defeat in the 2020 election.

news.title: Judge wants to know if Trump attorneys violated ethics in one of 2 cases to change the DC landscape
news.text: WASHINGTON, D.C. — A federal judge said Friday she would open a “formal inquiry” to investigate if attorneys for the Trump administration violated ethical boundaries during a legal dispute about a golf-course project — one in a pair of plans that are revealing the breadth of the president's attempts to mold parts of the District of Columbia to his own vision.The two cases, unfolding at the same time in the same federal courthouse, also showcase the underlying executive authority claims that lie beneath them — a glimpse into the uses of presidential power under Donald Trump.U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes' declaration that the court would appoint a “special master” to investigate whether agency officials and Justice Department attorneys had made misrepresentations in the court is a far cry from her relationship with the government until this month. She had rejected numerous motions from the plaintiffs to step in earlier, saying she trusted the government attorneys.The cases involved are an impending shutdown and reconfiguration of a historic public golf course and the construction of a monumental arch that, at 250 feet (75 meters), would be 100 feet taller than the Statue of Liberty is from its base to the top of the torch. The two projects are barely three miles, or five kilometers, apart.The hearing on the golf course change began as other recent ones have: Reyes grilled Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr. over how Trump’s desires to turn the golf course, near the National Mall, into a world-class facility have become urgent plans that match his public pronouncements.Reyes stopped the hearing several times and adjourned to her chambers to check previous transcripts of the trial as she questioned Woodward. Among the things she wants investigated: Was a National Park Service official told to exclude details in a court declaration? Did witnesses offer misleading testimony about the extent of plans in place for the course's closure and renovation?Reyes ordered Friday’s hearing after multiple Truth Social posts by Trump indicated that there were plans for the golf course and construction was expected to begin Nov. 15. Trump said the park would be closed for 15 months while work goes on.A flurry of Trump posts sets off chaosThe presidential posts, which began Oct. 18, created a tense dynamic in multiple court hearings afterward when officials from the Interior Department, Justice and National Park Service could not confirm the existence of the plans under questioning from Reyes. She eventually asked whom she should trust. The Justice Department filed notice Wednesday night that the plans were real.“On Friday, October 30, 2026, the National Park Service will submit to the National Capital Planning Commission for review a rendering designed by Tom Fazio for a World Class, championship-level golf course that is capable of hosting major events,' the notice said.Reyes locked in on the filing and Trump’s multiple Truth Social announcements as she questioned Woodward.At one point, as they talked about plans that Woodward said only came about this week, he slipped and included tree cutting as part of the preparation for the closure.Reyes responded immediately: “News flash.” She allowed him to correct himself that the tree cutting, which occurred earlier this month, was not part of the plan to close the East Potomac Golf Links.Another case is also a referendum on executive authorityThe golf course lawsuit was one of two cases in court Friday dealing with the Trump administration’s push to expand its executive authority as the president remakes the federal areas of the capital near the National Mall and along the Potomac River.Three courtrooms away, U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan questioned the Justice Department attorney extensively at a hearing prompted in part by the administration's court filing that it hoped to get final approval for the arch project on Nov. 5 and possibly begin construction that same day.The plaintiffs in the lawsuit challenging the construction asked for the preliminary injunction after the Oct. 21 court notification.Chutkan, like Reyes has in other hearings, asked what the urgency was and how would the government be harmed “apart from the executive's desire to bedazzle the city” if she issues a preliminary injunction while the lawsuit plays out. Robert Stander, the government's attorney, said the arch was “absolutely a high priority project” and Chutkan stepping in would impede the work of the government.Chutkan and Stander also engaged in a discussion over the recent court filings by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who talked about defensive structures, including drones, that will be part of the arch. Chutkan noted that it was the first time throughout the case that the government had framed the arch as a national defense matter. Stander had no details on what those defensive plans might entail.The government submitted a 106-page plan for the arch Friday that does not mention drones or defense. The plan depicts a massive arch more than 12 stories high that includes a huge bronze statue of Lady Liberty with wings and carrying a torch with an eternal flame. The structure will include an observation deck with views to the east and west, an “occupied roof” and two mezzanines.Inside the arch are rooms for program space, offices, a staff lounge, circular staircases, multiple elevators and a “fire command center.” The project proposes significant traffic changes in the area, including rerouting traffic on nearby roads..One of the plaintiffs, Michael Lemmon, an Army veteran who served as a helicopter pilot in Vietnam, said during testimony at the hearing that he routinely visits the Vietnam Veterans Memorial before walking toward the cemetery to pay respects to fallen comrades buried there. “It means an intense amount to me to be able to continue to do that,” he said. “The pain is real for us veterans. It’s not just an aesthetic (concern), not just some preference for a few.”Lemmon said he is disturbed by the prospect of seeing a “monstrous” arch loom over the cemetery.“This is hallowed ground. This is really sacred territory,” he said.Shaun Byrnes, a Navy veteran who was badly wounded while serving during the Vietnam War, said the arch’s construction would force him to reconsider his intention to be interred in Arlington National Cemetery along with former shipmates. In a court filing, Byrnes said he views the arch as a “symbol that violates our Nation’s resistance to the rule of a king and our Nation’s commitment to the rule of the people.”“I don’t want to be part of that,” he told Chutkan.The plaintiffs say the construction is unlawful and must be endorsed by Congress.Legal experts who have been watching the numerous cases underway say that what might appear at first glance to be vanity projects are in truth cases that test the limits of presidential power.Past administrations pursued legal theories that were sometimes legally sound, sometimes not, said David Super, law professor at the Georgetown University Law Center.“But there was always the assumption that you would try to do things that were legal,” he said. “What we’re seeing here now is that if you think the federal courts can’t stop you,” you can break the law.That’s ”going to do long-term damage to the country,” Super said.
news.author: Associated Press

news.title: Wall Street drops to its worst day since June after the sell-off for tech stocks deepens
news.text: NEW YORK — A sell-off for tech stocks got even worse Friday on worries that Wall Street’s frenzy around artificial-intelligence technology sent prices too high.The S&P 500 tumbled 1.8% for its worst day since June, and it closed out a third straight losing week. The weakness for technology stocks dragged the Nasdaq composite down a market-leading 2.9%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 572 points, or 1.1%.The U.S. stock market remains only 3.1% below its all-time high, which has boosted the value of workers’ 401(k) accounts, but it’s become increasingly shaky as Tuesday’s midterm elections in the United States approach. Worries about AI in general have already become a concern for voters across political parties, and President Donald Trump has historically used the stock market’s performance as a measure of his own success.Intel’s stock led the way lower and plunged 28.6% for its worst drop since 1974. The chipmaker gave a forecast for profit in the final three months of this year that fell short of analysts’ expectations, as CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the personal-computer industry continues to feel pressure. The drop came even though Intel reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected.Amazon fell 1.4% after reporting a weaker profit for the summer than analysts expected. Potentially more concerning for investors was Amazon’s reporting that it burned through $42.4 billion of cash over the prior 12 months, according to a measure called free cash flow. It spent $94.8 billion on property and equipment, primarily through investments in artificial-intelligence technology.A day earlier, Alphabet’s stock dropped more than 12% to its worst day on record and dragged the S&P 500 down after telling investors it burned through more cash during the summer than the spring. The company behind Google and YouTube cited similar, mammoth investments in AI.Worries are rising about whether all the hundreds of billions of dollars will produce enough profit and productivity to make the investment worth it. At the same time, stocks of computer chip companies and other winners from the frenzy to build AI data centers have come under pressure on concerns that high interest rates may slow the further build out of data centers.“We’re moving out of the hopes and dreams phase of the AI trade and into the ‘show me’ phase,” said Joe Tigay, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, in a note to investors.A drop of 4.2% for Nvidia, the chip company that became the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward, outweighing even Intel.In the cryptocurrency industry, meanwhile, stocks tumbled following a hack on the world’s biggest crypto exchange. The price of bitcoin fell below $77,000 from more than $86,000 earlier this month, and a U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm said a North Korean unit was likely behind the attack that impacted more than $6 billion worth of crypto at Binance.Coinbase Global fell 10.6% even though it reported stronger results for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Strategy, which says it owns about 4% of the total supply of bitcoin, fell 7.8%. It also reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected, while saying its chief financial officer will resign next week for personal reasons.Outside of tech, stocks were more resilient as many rallied after reporting stronger profits for the summer than analysts expected. Nearly as many stocks rose within the S&P 500 index as fell.ExxonMobil climbed 2.2%, and Chevron added 1.8% after the oil giants reported stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected.Mondelez International rose 3.9% after the company behind Oreo cookies and Ritz crackers reported stronger-than-expected growth.Colgate-Palmolive climbed 2.3% after higher prices for its products around much of the world helped it deliver better revenue and profit than analysts expected.Expectations are high for U.S. companies’ ability to make bigger profits, even though people around the world are feeling discouraged about high inflation and high fuel prices. Such expectations are what drove the S&P 500 to its record earlier this month.All told, the S&P 500 fell 140.32 points to 7,580.07. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 572.25 to 51,770.31, and the Nasdaq composite sank 747.73 to 25,437.00.In the bond market, Treasury yields eased in a signal that investors were buying U.S. government bonds in search of something safer to own. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93% from 4.98% late Thursday and from more than 5.30% earlier in the month.Treasury yields fell even though oil prices bounced higher, something that usually drives yields upward because it worsens inflation. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 2.4% to $113.43. It’s near the high end of its range since the war with Iran sent oil prices and inflation higher.In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe following sharper swings in Asia.South Korea’s Kospi dropped 3.5% as worries about AI hit its tech-heavy market, while the Hang Seng in Hong Kong climbed 1.5%.Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 2.1% after the Bank of Japan decided to keep interest rates steady, echoing moves made earlier in the week by the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank.
news.author: Associated Press

news.title: US-Iran deal on horizon? Uranium transfer, Hormuz reopening in 7 days proposed
news.text: NEW DELHI: A preliminary framework for negotiations between the United States and Iran proposes transferring Tehran's stockpile of highly enriched uranium to a third country or reducing its enrichment levels, alongside reopening the Strait of Hormuz to international shipping within seven days of an initial understanding, Al Arabiya English reported on Saturday.The draft framework, which was obtained exclusively by the news platform, also identifies China as a potential guarantor to ensure the implementation and sustainability of any agreement. It proposes holding direct negotiations between Washington and Tehran in Doha instead of Istanbul.Under the proposed arrangement, Iran would undertake commitments on its nuclear programme and maritime security in exchange for US steps to ease sanctions, blockades and other economic restrictions.The framework also envisages an independent verification mechanism to assess compliance before each phase of implementation. news.title: Trump boosts Donalds in Daytona Beach; Jolly reaches for undecided votes in final stretch of gubernatorial race
news.text:
(WSVN) - President Donald Trump made another campaign stop in Florida to stump for Republican gubernatorial candidate in a final blitz before Election Day. On the same day, Democratic candidate David Jolly was in Tampa Bay trying to drum up support from undecided voters.

With just four days left to sway voters’ minds on what direction to take Florida in, Byron Donalds brought in major reinforcements from the president once again to keep the governor’s mansion under Republican control for another four years.

The pair held a joint rally in Daytona Beach Friday night to drum up support for the upcoming midterm election.

Trump previously stumped for Donalds in Fort Myers last week, telling supporters he would make a “great governor” for Florida.

Though polls have consistently shown the 47-year-old ahead of Jolly, the race has seemingly tightened in the closing weeks.

Another show of support from Trump signals Republicans’ growing concerns that Jolly has managed to narrow the gap significantly after Gov. Ron DeSantis cruised to his 2022 reelection by just over 19 points against Charlie Crist.

Meanwhile, Jolly made a stop on the opposite coast of Central Florida in Tampa Bay, meeting with undecided voters in an attempt to persuade them on his quest to become the first Democrat to become Florida governor since 1994.

news.title: Trump’s Florida Rally Interrupted by Protesters in Final Midterm Blitz
news.text: President Donald Trump used a Friday night rally in Florida to tout Republican candidates Byron Donalds and Ashley Moody, announce additional hurricane funding for the state and unleash a string of attacks on Democrats, actor Robert De Niro and audience hecklers. Trump has been campaigning for a solid month in hopes of elevating Republican candidates in the midterms. Polls are tight in many states as Democrats hope to take control of the Senate and House. "We have to win in four days, and it means everybody in our state needs to go out and vote," Donalds told the crowd. "There will be no sharia law here in Florida. We gotta get out and vote. We gotta get out and win. We gotta keep Florida free." Trump Highlights FEMA Funding for Florida Trump told supporters he recently approved an additional $184 million in FEMA disaster funding for Florida's Panhandle after requests from Donalds and Moody. "Could we get $184 million in additional FEMA hurricane relief funding for the Florida Panhandle?" Trump recalled being asked. "I love the Panhandle." The declaration covered 15 counties in northwest Florida that suffered damage in Hurricane Isaias. Residents are eligible for federal assistance, including temporary housing, home repairs and other recovery aid. Trump Says Hollywood Critics Are Now Seeking His Help In one of the night's more unexpected detours, Trump claimed entertainment industry figures who have spent years criticizing him are now privately asking for federal help as film and television production increasingly moves overseas. Trump suggested he may support tax credits aimed at keeping production in the United States. "Guys that have been saying bad crap about me for years are sitting up in my office. 'Sir, it's a great honor to be with you, sir,'" Trump said. He argued that countries including Canada, Australia and the United Kingdom have lured productions away from Hollywood through government incentives. Trump singled out actor Robert De Niro. "Is Robert De Niro a moron? He's a moron," Trump said. "No, there's something wrong with him." Trump went on to say he once liked De Niro's work but now finds him "gross" and criticized some of his more recent performances. The two have been exchanging insults for nearly a decade. Newsweek reached out to De Niro's agent for comment. Trump Fires Off a String of Insults at Democrats The president also spent significant portions of the rally targeting Democratic politicians and political opponents. Among them was Texas state Representative James Talarico, whom Trump called "a freak" while joking about his veganism. Talarico has leaned into being called a "freak" after being called such by his opponent Ken Paxton, with supporters donning "Tala-freak-o" merch. Talarico has also denied that he is a vegan, a false claim that Republicans repeat. Trump also attacked former Republican-turned-Democrat David Jolly, calling him a "freaking loser" while criticizing his positions on guns and immigration. He described Florida state Representative Angie Nixon as "a very low IQ person" and used the speech to renew attacks on Representative Ilhan Omar, saying she should resign from Congress. Trump also took aim at Michigan Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed, again calling him "a jihadist" as he warned supporters against backing Democratic candidates he described as extremists. El-Sayed responded on X on October 8 to similar accusations by Trump, saying, "He knows my name is Abdul. He says it everyday. But he’s not just attacking me. He’s attacking all of us. He thinks so low of us. He thinks he can use my name and my faith to distract us from the suffering his policies are inflicting on us at the pump, at the grocery store, and at the doctor’s office. He thinks we don’t know any better." Trump argued that Jewish and Black voters should not support the Michigan Democrat. "If you're black or if you're Jewish and you vote for Abdul, you're not smart," Trump said. "Abdul is not a big fan of Jewish people and he's not a big fan of black people... I hope you're going to vote against him and send him back to where he came from." However, while on the campaign trail, El-Sayed has visited several Black congregations. Along the way, he held a town hall at the Shrine of the Black Madonna to acknowledge the "tensions" between Black and Arab Americans, the Religion News Service reported. While there, he borrowed from Martin Luther King Jr.’s “I Have a Dream” speech, saying, “I also ask that I am judged by the content of my character, not the color of my skin,” he said at the September 14 event, drawing applause. Newsweek reached out to El-Sayed's campaign for comment. Trump Spars With Hecklers Protesters interrupted the speech several times, prompting Trump to stop and address them directly. Trump responded: "Loser! What a loser!" Later, during remarks on immigration, he pointed to another demonstrator and dismissed him as "that dope." The exchanges drew cheers from supporters and became a recurring theme throughout the rally. He complained that news organizations have historically downplayed his crowd sizes, while highlighting attendance at events held by political rivals, including Senator Bernie Sanders. "They don't want to mention my crowd size because crowd size means success," Trump said. Woman Arrested for Threatening Trump Hours prior to the rally, Florida authorities arrested a 21-year-old woman for threatening on social media to shoot Trump during the Daytona Beach rally. Allison Albro posted a selfie on Instagram with a caption reading: “Going to the trump rally in my city tmr so I can shoot him with my Glock! Wish me luck guys!!,” according to Volusia County Sheriff Mike Chitwood. "Today she’s sitting in jail on charges of written threats to kill and unlawful use of a communications device. I would strongly advise anyone else thinking of posting a 'joke' along these lines to think twice," he wrote. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. news.title: U.S. approves $2.1B Patriot missile sale to Ukraine
news.text:
The U.S. State Department said today it had approved the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1 billion, in what would be one of the most significant steps to supply defensive weapons to Kyiv since the start of the second Trump administration.

Delayed missile deliveries have added to Ukraine’s tensions with the U.S. after President Donald Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia and criticised Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for Ukraine’s unwillingness to stop attacks on Russian refineries.

Ukraine has long said it urgently needs more missile interceptors to knock down the growing waves of missiles Russia’s military fires at the country. The Patriot missile system is the most effective weapon to counter fast-moving ballistic missiles.

On Thursday, a Russian drone strike killed at least 14 people on a crowded rail platform in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro, while 5 died in daytime strikes on two other provincial cities and a late-evening missile strike killed 1 person in the capital Kyiv, officials said.

Zelenskyy said on Monday that Ukraine had been waiting for almost a month for the U.S. to sign off on critical missile supplies, as Russia stepped up attacks on energy and civilian infrastructure.

But despite Ukraine’s urgency, it will likely not receive the missile interceptors quickly. Weapons sales typically take years to fulfill, and two people briefed on the U.S. decision said the missiles — which are yet to be manufactured — are not expected to be delivered until a couple of years into the 2030s.

One of the people said Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense is encouraging the Pentagon to bring forward the delivery date, possibly by giving Kyiv missiles already in the U.S. arsenal and back-filling with the new Patriot interceptors.

Ukraine will pay for the missiles with contributions from Canada, Germany and Norway routed through a program called U.S. JUMPSTART, along with national funds financed by the European Union’s Ukraine Support Loan, the State Department said in a statement.

The program uses donations from allies to buy weapons, services and training for Ukraine to support its self-defense following Russia’s invasion, according to a Pentagon website.

The JUMPSTART program was used in August to buy 3,350 air-launched cruise missiles worth $825 million made by Zone 5 Technologies and CoAspire.

Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor for the sale of the Patriot interceptors.

The U.S. has supplied large quantities of weapons to allies while also using munitions in its own military operations in Iran, raising concerns about inventories of key air defense and precision-guided weapons.

In July, the U.S. Army awarded Lockheed a contract worth up to $58.6 billion to produce Patriot interceptor missiles.

Lockheed has said that deal would allow it to follow through on a promise to triple PAC-3 MSE production capacity by the end of 2030 and increase jobs at its Camden, Arkansas, plant by 50%, to about 1,850 from 1,200. Lockheed previously announced Patriot PAC-3 missile interceptor production would go to 2,000 units annually.

Pentagon negotiators are pressing contractors to move much faster, with tentative production agreements struck earlier this year at the center of efforts to increase missile output.
news.summary: The U.S. State Department said today it had approved the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1 billion, in what would be one of the most significant steps to supply defensive weapons to Kyiv since the start of the second Trump administration.

news.title: Trump Drums Up Boos for Fox News in Rally Rant
news.text:
Donald Trump has whined about Fox News at a Florida rally, drumming up boos for the right-wing network that he says is giving too much airtime to Democrats.

Trump, 80, raged at Fox News while speaking in Daytona Beach, where he complained that, in the lead-up to the midterms, the network is giving opponents of his endorsed candidates too much time on air.

Trump specifically took issue with seeing California Rep. Ro Khanna on Fox and Friends earlier that morning.

“I watched this total dope, Ro Khanna. Fox puts him on all the time. You know, Fox is giving Democrats more time than they’re giving Republicans. I don’t know what the hell is—,” he said, drawing boos from the crowd. “I’m working my a-- off, I’m doing rallies, and I come back and I watch the opponent of the person I did the rally for. I’m—I’m not happy.”

This week, Trump criticized Fox on Truth Social for interviewing Democrats like Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and Iowa gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand. Republican candidates, he grumbled, are getting “blurred out.”

“FoxNews is spending far too much time putting on the OPPONENTS of Republican Party Candidates, people that love our Country, and have Great Policies and Ideas,” Trump posted, saying the network was “trying too hard to be Politically Correct.”

The tension comes as Fox is reportedly on track to have its lowest-rated month since December 2023. That may be due to Trump fatigue, as one Fox host told CNN that the internal consensus is that Trump “doesn’t rate anymore.” 

Fox aired every second of Trump’s 90-minute speech on Friday. That included multiple hecklers interrupting him, and his bizarre closing message to voters—including him taking time to rage that Academy Award winners do not like him and to tell Robert DeNiro he is not cracked up for comedy roles.

news.title: The Republican senator campaigning on her clashes with Trump
news.text:
As the US midterm elections get closer, Donald Trump's polling numbers keep diving further underwater.

And Republican Senate candidates are becoming more vocal about their differences with the president.

Michigan's Mike Rogers, an early tariffs supporter, is now calling for an end to the Canada trade war.

New Hampshire's John Sununu, who initially praised Trump's decision to attack Iran, now criticises the plan as flawed.

And Ohio's Jon Husted, who has championed data centres for years, now says they should only be built where the locals want them.

But in Maine, Susan Collins can lay claim to a long history of disagreements with Trump.

The veteran Republican, a fixture of the Senate since Bill Clinton was president, even voted to convict Trump after he was impeached over the January 6 insurrection.

"I'm not exactly his favourite senator," she said during one recent debate. 

"I vote very independently," she told another.

Talking up her differences with Trump is a central part of Collins's strategy to keep her seat. It could be the key to helping his Republican Party keep control of the Senate.

Lost support

Republicans see the Maine Senate seat as one they cannot afford to lose.

The local polls are hairbreadth tight, but Trump is unpopular in Maine. About twice as many Mainers disapprove of his performance than approve, according to Civiqs' public opinion tracker.

So the question is: Has Collins done enough to convince Mainers she will stand up to Trump when it counts?

For Lee Umphrey, who had consistently voted for Collins up until this year, the answer is no.

"I've known her a long time, she's done a lot of good, and for organisations like ours she has been very reliable," said Umphrey, who runs a community development corporation in Bangor, where Collins lives.

"[But] this is really a referendum on President Trump's executive power and the abuses connected to that."

He listed examples including the Elon Musk-led slashing of government services, cuts to Medicaid health insurance under the "Big Beautiful Bill", tariffs on Canada, and the war in Iran.

'Women felt betrayed'

To some extent, Collins split with Trump on all four examples listed by Umphrey. 

She voiced opposition to some DOGE cuts, voted against the Big Beautiful Bill, criticised the Canada tariffs, and supported Democrat-led resolutions to end the war.

She points to wins like her successful efforts to boost rural health funding in the Big Beautiful Bill and to remove tariffs from some Canadian products, including rock salt used on Maine's icy roads in winter.

Her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, mocks what he sees as meek efforts for meagre concessions. 

"She's like an arsonist who helped set the fire and then she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out," he said in one recent debate.

Her critics argue she too often caves to pressure.

"I'm sure that she has done good things for the state of Maine and for the country, but of late, ever since Trump has been on the scene, she's mostly been complicit," said Mary Ann Larson, part of a group that holds weekly protests against Collins and Trump.

Like many in Maine, Larson has not forgotten Collins's role in appointing Supreme Court judges that overturned abortion rights, including her critical vote to confirm Trump-nominee Brett Kavanaugh's appointment in 2018.

"So many women felt betrayed by that," Larson said. "We're half the population and we basically were disenfranchised by that vote."

Local issues

Collins has a history of outperforming the polls.

When she was last up for election six years ago, polls predicted she would lose. But she won by nine percentage points.

Democrats' hopes for her defeat were high again earlier this year, as candidate Graham Platner attracted a huge groundswell of grassroots support.

But he was forced out of the race in July after being accused of sexual assault (which he denies).

One of the biggest blows to Collins's campaign came in September, when ProPublica published an investigation into alleged bribery.

Jackson called it "corruption of the highest order" but Collins denied wrongdoing, and the allegations do not look to have significantly dented her re-election effort.

Some of Collins's enduring electoral success is attributed to her work on low-key local issues and dealings with constituents. 

Some locals offer personal stories when asked for their views on the senator, like Bangor local Lisa Thomas, who said she had bumped into Collins several times at the shops.

"About four years ago we were talking about pot roasts, and she gave me her mother's recipe. I've used it ever since, and it's great," said Thomas.

"Each time I see her, I always come to shake her hand and say, 'I appreciate you, I appreciate what you stand for, for goodness and equality.'"

Broken promises

Thomas was collecting a Susan Collins lawn sign at a family day for conservatives at a Bangor church, co-sponsored by the Republican Party.

Handing out the signs was 19-year-old volunteer Sofia Pride, who described Collins as "easy to support whichever side of the political spectrum you're on".

"I've always looked up to her," she said, recalling how Collins used to phone into a public radio show Pride worked on when she was at high school.

But when asked about Trump, Pride said: "I'm going to pass on the question if that's OK. I think it's not about him right now. It's about having Senator Collins win this race, and he's chosen not to be involved in it, and I think that says a lot."

Some attendees said they would vote for Collins despite having reservations about Trump.

"When he ran in 2024, he promised us no new wars," said three-time Trump voter Michael Capeci.

"Then he made the decision to go to war in Iran for supposed nuclear weapons that I don't think even exist.

"But I strongly support Susan Collins because she's delivered a lot of good money to the state of Maine and she's done so much to keep businesses open and get economic development and federal funds into the state."

Trump's 11th-hour gift

Collins's campaign has focused on promoting her as a fighter for local causes as much as it has promoted her fights with Trump.

And the Trump administration delivered a gift to boost those messages in the final days of the campaign.

Last week, Collins announced the White House had agreed to another reduction on tariffs on Canadian products, including those deemed crucial to Maine's famed blueberry and apple industries.

The move could indicate Trump and his team fear his unpopularity could finally spell the end of Collins's electoral luck.

"There's a growing resentment that while he's doing well and the stock market's happy and his rich friends are happy, people on the street are hurting," said Umphrey, the community development head.

"We're seeing this all the time with diesel fuel, regular gasoline, food costs, healthcare costs all going up.

"I think any goodwill that Senator Collins has built up because of her good work is going to fade away, because it's pretty severe."
news.summary: Donald Trump desperately wants to retain a Republican majority in the US Senate. He is banking on the success of a senator whose campaign tactics include talking up her differences with the president.

news.title: Trump Melts Down as Heckler Spoils His Rally
news.text:
President Donald Trump has melted down on stage after a heckler interrupted him mid-sentence during a Florida rally.

Trump was interrupted by a screaming heckler in the opening minutes of his rally in Daytona Beach, Florida—but microphones did not pick up what the protester was yelling from the rafters.

The 80-year-old Trump’s meltdown, however, could be heard loud and clear.

“Shut up! Shut up, dope!” Trump raged. “Shut up, loser! What a loser.”

“Get him out of here,” Trump continued.

Trump then went silent, shaking his head in annoyance while the crowd cheered the security guards on. 

It was not the only interjection during the rally, with Trump labeling another protester as paid. 

“Paid protester,” he yelled out as security escorted them out. “Paid protester.” 

“We have it all down, we have the names, we have everything. The source. So they get $250, and then they get booked at a precinct, and they ruin their lives. How stupid are they?” he said.

“I’ve said it before,” Trump continued. “He goes home, he sees his mother, she smacks him in the face, says I voted for that guy; don’t you ever do that again. Don’t you ever do it. Don’t you do it again, darling.”

Trump has appeared visibly annoyed on stage as hecklers have repeatedly interrupted him this month. 

 In Kansas, they interrupted his speech six times. In Ohio, a screaming protester reminded everyone: “Trump went on the Jeffrey Epstein plane!” In Mississippi, a heckler told Trump to “shove that ballroom up your fat a--!”

Trump was interrupted by hecklers a third time on Friday about 40 minutes into his rambling rally speech, which included him venting about the Academy Awards (because winners dare to criticize him) and why he thinks Robert De Niro should not do comedy. 

Trump also repeated his most bizarre closing message to voters this cycle—commenting about the physique of Ohio Sen. Jon Husted. Husted is a former college football player, whose butt the president cannot stop talking about.

news.title: ‘The View’ co-hosts say Dems shouldn’t impeach Trump if they regain control of Congress

“The View” co-hosts agreed with former Vice President Kamala Harris Friday that impeachment would not be a good use of the Democratic Party’s time and resources if the party wins back control of Congress in the midterm elections.

“I think that going on in the direction of impeachment is not a good idea,” Harris warned Tuesday on “The Parnas Perspective” podcast. “OK, just to be honest with you. Because we have limited resources, and I think the energy and the resources need to be put into accountability, need to be put into investigations. And that’s where the time should be spent. Remember, I was in the Senate for the last go-round and the votes aren’t there, right? So, that’s how I feel.”

After playing a clip of Harris’ comments, “The View” co-hosts agreed with her assessment.

“In terms of Trump, no, I don’t think that’s what should be on the agenda,” co-host Sunny Hostin said. “Hakeem Jeffries — who I believe will be the next speaker of the House, after November — he has a plan for 100 days which includes tax credits, taking care of the tax credits, limiting ICE and also stock trades. 

“And then he’s got a plan for the first 100 hours, which would include, you know, just undoing a lot of unpopular Trump policies. So, I think there is a plan in place that Democrats have, and it may not include impeaching Trump.”

“I think that Democrats have to be realistic of what’s achievable,” co-host Ana Navarro said. “We are four days away from the election. So, before we start talking about what Democrats are going to do once they win, they’ve got to make sure they win. 

“People have to focus not on all of the conversation about impeachment and what is going to happen but rather on getting out the vote and getting people to the polls so that the American people decide who they want in power in the House and in the Senate.

“There’s a limit to what Democrats are going to be able to do even if they win the House, even if they win the House and the Senate, because Donald Trump is still president,” she continued. “Legislation in this country needs to be signed by the president. If not, it needs to have a veto-proof majority. And I think that’s going to be very difficult to achieve. I’m completely against impeachment.

“There’s 100 other ways to hold Donald Trump and his administration accountable,” Navarro added. “Impeachment is an exercise that’s moot if you don’t have the 67 votes in the Senate required to indict.”

Joy Behar pointed to former President Richard Nixon’s resignation from office after Republican lawmakers warned him that he lacked sufficient Senate support to avoid conviction if impeached and said of Trump, “If we don’t have the votes to convict, there’s no point in impeaching.”

Sara Haines also agreed, arguing that many of Trump’s supporters are now angry with him for breaking campaign promises and that Democrats could capitalize on their dissatisfaction by delivering on their own promises.

“It’s important to recognize the moment,” she said. “Donald Trump was elected and promised things he never touched. He’s been remodeling, redecorating, working to revenge, all the things. The voters were left high and dry, which is why we’re seeing some red states flip full to blue,” she said. “That’s why we are watching this campaigning.

“They need to see someone get in there, hold them accountable, do the investigations, fine,” Haines continued. “But really show the American people that what they promised, to fix all these things, that immediately there’s action taken. Even if it can’t get past the president. Spin the wheels. Show the people that you are putting up policy, that you are taking things to vote, that you are actually acting for the people that put you there.”

“Impeachment is not where the focus should be,” Alyssa Farah Griffin said. “It costs actually a lot of money to do a trial, do the investigation.

“What I think is important is there are day one things that would be beneficial for all Americans and a lot of Republicans would be on board with that a Democratic Congress could do,” she continued.

“Repealing Trump’s tariffs, that is the power of the purse controlled by Congress and trying to wind down or pause the war in Iran. Those are things you should get Republican votes to do. That will bring down people’s fuel prices. Those are where the focus should be.”

Earlier this month, veteran Democratic strategist James Carville also warned Democrats against impeaching Trump if the party wins control of Congress in the midterms.

Democratic strategist and co-host of “The Huddle” podcast Dan Turrentine told Fox News Digital, “Neither the Senate arithmetic nor the American people are there. Folks are angry with the president about the economy, tariffs, healthcare, the war with Iran, corruption. They feel he is focused on everything but them.

“Our job is to fight for the real lives of real people, solving their problems, while providing appropriate oversight of the executive branch and trusting the electorate provides accountability,” he added. 

“The quickest path back to the minority or continuing to be on the outside, looking into the White House, is to focus on revenge and score settling.”
news.summary: "The View" co-hosts agreed with Kamala Harris that Democrats should focus on policy and investigations rather than impeaching President Donald Trump.

She said the message was plain: Trump’s presence could hurt Republicans more than it helps.

She said Republicans in those states likely felt relieved not to have to appear with him, and that some tried to spin it as strength. Asked about the Kansas cancellation, Marshall said, “I think they think that by doing so well in the polls that he’s probably got better places to spend his time.”

“Oh, my,” Psaki said, noting Marshall is trailing Democrat Adam Hamilton by more than three points in the polling average in a state that hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate in almost 100 years. “We can see the polls, too, senator.”

news.title: China backs South Africa after US leaves it out of G20 ministerial in Atlanta
news.text: Digital Desk | Atlanta, Oct 31 (IANS) China has backed South Africa’s continued participation in the G20 after the United States left Pretoria out of the grouping’s foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta, setting up a fresh point of friction as Washington hosts the forum this year. “South Africa is an important member of the G20. China supports South Africa in continuing its participation in G20 activities,” Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a regular press conference in Beijing on Friday, according to the ministry’s official transcript. Guo was responding to a question from state broadcaster CCTV, which noted that South Africa, a founding member of the G20, “was once again not invited” to the Atlanta meeting. “As a major platform for international economic cooperation, the G20 plays an important role in strengthening multilateralism, promoting world economic growth, and improving global governance,” Guo said. The ministry’s spokesperson account repeated the remarks on X under the heading “MFA Spokesperson’s response to South Africa’s exclusion from G20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in the U.S.” The US decision dates back to last year. In an article published by the State Department on December 4, 2025, Secretary of State Marco Rubio wrote: “For these reasons, President Trump and the United States will not be extending an invitation to the South African government to participate in the G20 during our presidency. There is a place for good faith disagreement, but not dishonesty or sabotage.” Rubio said South Africa’s G20 presidency “was an exercise in spite, division, and radical agendas that have nothing to do with economic growth” and that it “routinely ignored U.S. objections to consensus communiques and statements.” “When South Africa decides it has made the tough decisions needed to fix its broken system and is ready to rejoin the family of prosperous and free nations, the United States will have a seat for it at our table,” he wrote. South Africa has rejected the US position. In a statement dated November 26, 2025, published by the Department of International Relations and Cooperation (DIRCO), the government said President Cyril Ramaphosa had “noted the regrettable statement by President Donald Trump on South Africa’s participation in the 2026 G20 meetings.” “South Africa is a member of the G20 in its own name and right,” the statement said. “South Africa will continue to participate as a full, active and constructive member of the G20. We call on members of the G20 to reaffirm its continued operation in the spirit of multilateralism, based on consensus, with all members participating on an equal footing in all of its structures.” DIRCO had not issued a statement specifically on the Atlanta meeting as of Friday afternoon (US time). The State Department has not publicly addressed South Africa’s absence in its announcement of the Atlanta meeting, which Rubio is hosting on October 30 and 31.

news.title: Explosions in Hormuz as Trump says Iran ‘wants to talk’
news.text: A series of maritime incidents and reported explosions in the Persian Gulf heightened tensions between Iran and the United States on Friday, even as President Donald Trump said Tehran was seeking negotiations and Washington was in no hurry to reach an agreement. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed that four oil tankers had struck naval mines and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after ignoring Iranian navigation warnings, while British maritime authorities reported separate incidents involving vessels struck by unidentified projectiles. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency (UKMTO) said a vessel was hit on its port side by an unidentified projectile approximately 40 nautical miles (74 kilometers) south of Iran's Lavan Island in the Persian Gulf. The impact sparked a fire on board, but the crew was reported safe and no environmental damage had been reported. The vessel's identity and the party responsible for the incident remained unknown. In a separate report, UKMTO said an oil tanker had been struck by an unidentified projectile while leaving the Strait of Hormuz. The agency did not identify those responsible for the attack. Iran claims four tankers hit mines after ignoring warnings Iran's Revolutionary Guards said four oil tankers had caught fire following explosions in the strategically vital waterway. According to the IRGC Navy, the fourth tanker was carrying more than two million barrels of crude oil when it struck a naval mine, triggering a powerful explosion and fire. Iranian officials claimed the tankers had attempted to cross the strait using routes not authorized by Tehran and that at least some had ignored repeated warnings from Iranian forces. Iranian state media also reported that some vessels had switched off their navigation and tracking systems before entering dangerous areas. The claims could not be independently verified. It remained unclear whether the vessels mentioned in the British maritime warnings were among the four tankers cited by Iran's Revolutionary Guards. Meanwhile, Omani authorities said they had evacuated 25 crew members from a Panama-flagged tanker that was attacked and caught fire near the coast of Musandam governorate, close to the Strait of Hormuz. Authorities did not immediately establish whether the vessel was among those mentioned by Iran. The latest incidents underscore the continuing threat to commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most important maritime chokepoints. Under normal circumstances, roughly one-fifth of global oil supplies pass through the narrow waterway connecting the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman. Since the war began in late February, Iran has intensified its efforts to control shipping through the strait, repeatedly warning that vessels attempting to cross without its authorization risk being attacked. Trump: ‘They want to talk, we have time’ Against the backdrop of escalating maritime tensions, Trump said Friday that diplomatic contacts with Tehran were continuing and emphasized that Washington was under no immediate pressure to reach an agreement. "There are talks. They want to talk. They keep talking," Trump told reporters at the White House. "We have time, frankly." Trump described the conflict with Iran as "not a typical war" and claimed it was not imposing significant costs on American taxpayers. He also repeated his assertion that U.S. military operations had eliminated Iran's nuclear threat. "I spent a lot of money in order to get rid of a nuclear weapon, which we've done," he said. Earlier Friday, in an interview with Kansas City radio station KCMO, Trump expressed optimism that the confrontation would soon end. "It will end soon," he said, without explaining how an agreement might be reached. The president reiterated that Washington's central demand for ending the conflict remained a guarantee that Iran would never possess nuclear weapons. His remarks came just days before the U.S. midterm elections, scheduled for Tuesday, November 3. Trump has previously indicated that he would not order additional strikes against Iran before the elections, but has stopped short of ruling out renewed military action afterward. According to a report published by the Associated Press this week, U.S. officials warned several Middle Eastern countries and regional allies to prepare for the possibility of renewed strikes against Iran following the elections. The warnings also addressed the prospect of Iranian retaliation, potentially targeting energy facilities and other critical infrastructure across the region. Two diplomats briefed on the discussions stressed, however, that Trump had not made a final decision on whether to resume military operations. Qatar pushes for a deal as fears of renewed US strikes grow As tensions mounted in the Gulf, diplomatic efforts to avert another round of fighting continued Friday with the arrival of a Qatari delegation in Tehran. According to Iran's official IRNA news agency, the delegation was headed by a senior adviser to Qatar's prime minister and was expected to meet senior Iranian officials to discuss bilateral relations and regional developments. A source familiar with the negotiations told Reuters that Qatar's mediation efforts were being coordinated with the Trump administration. Qatar had presented Iran with a draft agreement on Sunday aimed at ending the war, but a senior Iranian official dismissed the proposals as unacceptable and said Tehran would not change its position on the nuclear issue. The main obstacle remains the sequence of steps toward a possible agreement. Washington insists that Iran's nuclear program be addressed from the beginning of negotiations, while Tehran is demanding that the United States first lift its blockade of Iranian ports and remove sanctions restricting Iranian oil exports. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday that Tehran remained in close contact with mediators and was reviewing proposals that could help advance an Iranian seven-day plan for ending the conflict. He stressed that Iran was still giving diplomacy a chance, despite the substantial differences separating the two sides. The mediation efforts have also been accompanied by a more direct American approach. According to reports, U.S. Vice President JD Vance sent a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, as Washington explored possible diplomatic channels. Iranian authorities confirmed receiving the letter but said they had not yet responded. U.S. media reports indicated that the correspondence concerned the possibility of renewing negotiations, potentially establishing a framework for direct talks between Washington and Tehran. Trump, however, offered a different explanation Thursday, saying the purpose of the outreach was to discuss the delivery of medical supplies and humanitarian assistance to Iran. With Qatar pressing ahead on the diplomatic front and Washington weighing its options after the midterm elections, the gap between the two sides remains substantial. The tanker fires and explosions reported in the Strait of Hormuz have added another dangerous complication to negotiations already overshadowed by the possibility of renewed U.S. military action.
news.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards claim four tankers struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz, while British monitors report vessels hit by unidentified projectiles; Qatari mediators arrive in Tehran as Washington considers renewed strikes following the US midterm elections
