news.title: ANDREW NEIL: If Trump gets a bloody nose in Tuesday's midterms, he will only be MORE nasty and deranged than ever
news.text:
Those who detest Donald Trump, in America and beyond, are almost salivating at the prospect that he’ll get not one but two bloody noses in Tuesday’s midterm elections.

Their expectations are likely to be satisfied.

That Trump’s Republican Party will lose control of the House of Representatives is as certain as anything can be in American politics these days.

The loss of the Senate is not so clear cut, though it’s looking that way too.

If it happens, and both elected chambers on Capitol Hill fall under the control of the Democrats, there will be no disguising the humiliation for a President who does not handle electoral defeat well.

But if his enemies think even two bloody noses will cause him to slink away, diminished and dejected, to spend his remaining two years in the Oval Office as a lame-duck President, licking his wounds and unable to do very much (bar, perhaps, finish that blingy White House ballroom), then they are in for the surprise of their lives.

US Presidents still wield enormous power, at home and abroad, even if they don’t control Congress. That will be especially true of a post-midterm Trump, who hasn’t bothered much with Congress even when his party was in charge of the House and the Senate.

Defeat on Tuesday is likely to make him more unpredictable, more reckless, more self-obsessed – above all more dangerous – than ever. All the more so because a Democratic-controlled Congress will be out for revenge on so many fronts – policy, personal, family, business – making Trump all the more angry and aggressive.

Far from a period of quiet in which Trump largely bides his time until America chooses a new President in 2028, I fear US politics is about to become more unstable, more nasty, more deranged than ever, with consequences that will reverberate well beyond US borders.

Friends and foes alike in the rest of the world, including Britain, should brace themselves for two years of even more turmoil and upheaval.

So, though Tuesday night will be tough for Trump as the results come in – the only unknown is how tough – I would counsel his enemies to contain their celebrations. Even in defeat, Trump will remain the dominant force in America – and therefore in geopolitics.

The loss of the House will be nothing exceptional. The current Republican majority is minuscule and the party in control of the White House usually loses the House come the midterms.

There have been only three exceptions to that rule since 1900 – 1934, 1998 and 2002. Trump is not about to achieve a fourth.

But there will be no ‘blue wave’ sweeping the Democrats to power in a landslide.

Indeed, I doubt they’ll even do as well as they did in the 2018 midterms during Trump’s first presidency, when they flipped 41 seats to take the House.

But they will flip enough seats – at least 20, maybe 30 if it’s a good night – to grant them a modest working majority in the House, giving them control of all its powerful investigative and oversight committees, which will make Trump’s tenure increasingly uncomfortable.

The Senate is another matter.

Unlike the House, the party incumbent in the White House has often done well in midterm Senate elections. Only 35 of its 100 seats are up for grabs in the midterms (whereas every House seat is contested) and the Republicans are helped by so many of the ‘toss up’ seats being in states Trump won convincingly in 2024.

There isn’t a lot of low-hanging fruit for the Democrats.

Their hopes are highest in Ohio, Maine, Alaska, Texas and Iowa. Trump won in every one of these states two years ago by between 11 and 13 points.

The Democrats are ahead in the Senate race polls in all five; but by only small margins. They need to win at least four Senate seats to take control.

There’s a lot in their favour. Trump’s approval ratings are in the dirt. His war on Iran has made him even more unpopular. It has pushed up the price of petrol and diesel to record levels, elevating cost-of-living concerns to the top of the agenda once more.

It’s estimated the war has added $1,000 to the costs of the average household. Trump’s tariffs have added another $1,000.

The US economy continues to defy the destructive shenanigans of its political class and grow strongly. But the benefits are skewed to the wealthiest 10 per cent, who are not the folks who vote for Trump.

The authoritative University of Michigan consumer sentiment index finds the economic mood among Americans the lowest it’s ever been in the run up to midterm elections since its index was established in the early 1950s. Wage growth after inflation has been stagnant since Trump was re-elected in 2024.

The MAGA cult is sticking with him. But so many of the voting groups that gave him victory only two years ago – Hispanics, independents, moderate Republicans – have deserted him.

In 2024, Trump won 44 per cent of the Hispanic vote. The Democrats had only an 11-point lead among Hispanics, which was a historic low. It’s now a 30-point lead. Independents have turned their backs on Trump by even more: only 23 per cent of these voters now approve of him.

As a result, even the Senate seat up for election in Kansas, which hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, is now too close to call.

The one Senate seat currently held by the Democrats that the Republicans have hopes of taking is in Michigan. The Democrats have not helped themselves by choosing an Islamo-Leftist as their candidate. But it looks as if they will hold on to it.

The best the Republicans can hope for is a 50:50 split in the Senate, which means they still hold on to it because Vice President JD Vance, as presiding officer, has the casting vote. The mood in the White House is grim. Trump has taken to raging against all and sundry whenever bad news lands.

The place is divided into factions, people are polishing their CVs for life after Trump. Susie Wiles, his chief of staff and the most sensible of his closest advisers, is considering quitting.

But that will make no difference to Trump. He will become even more his own man. So what if I’m a bit unpopular, he’ll say. Folks hate Congress even more. And he’s right. Americans come close to despising Congress. Even in defeat, Trump will not let it constrain him.

He’s already contemplating a resumption of major hostilities against Iran. To what purpose, nobody is quite sure. There are few around him who think it right. But that won’t stop him. Oil prices are already rising again in anticipation. The Gulf States are in despair.

Trump is also thinking of his legacy. President Putin has dangled the prospect of a Yalta-style conference of the Big Three. At Yalta in 1945, America, Russia and Britain agreed on the post-war carve-up of Europe.

Putin proposes today’s Big Three – America, Russia and China – determine the direction of today’s world. Trump is inclined to participate. It appeals to his vanity.

He’s anxious to restore normal relations with Russia to the financial advantage of his family and his cronies. If Ukraine has to be sacrificed in the process, so be it. Trump has never much cared for Ukraine. Even a Democratic Congress will not be able to stop him.

Then there’s Cuba. Its communist regime presides over an economic basketcase. Trump thinks his place in history will be guaranteed if he can bring it down – or at least force it to bend to America’s will, much as he’s done in Venezuela.

One commentator, who understands defeat on Tuesday will not see Trump go quietly into the night, has said that post-midterms he’ll be like an ageing, angry, silver-backed gorilla. But gorillas are only dangerous if threatened.

Trump will be more like a bull in a China shop, rampaging around, causing chaos wherever his fancy takes him. Desperate to leave his mark, doing what he wants because nobody can stop him and, with no need to be re-elected, nothing to lose.

By all means, if you are so inclined, enjoy his comeuppance on Tuesday. Then steel yourself for worse to come.
news.summary: Those who detest Donald Trump are almost salivating at the prospect that he'll get two bloody noses in Tuesday's midterm elections. But he will not slink away, diminished and dejected.
news.author: Andrew Neil,Editor

news.title: ‘Deeply Worried’ Republican Senator Sounds Doomsday Alarm for Midterms
news.text:
Ted Cruz is warning that Republicans are staring down a midterm wipeout in Congress and across the state of Texas. 

Cruz said on his podcast he is “deeply, deeply worried” about the vote totals so far. As of Friday, four days out from Election Day, over 48 million mail-in and early in-person votes had been cast, with 47 percent being by registered Democrats and just 35 percent by Republicans.

The Texas senator has acknowledged that disdain for Trump is driving the GOP’s doomsday scenario.

“What we’re seeing across the country is massive Democrat turnout. Democrats are showing up. They’re energized,” Cruz said. “They hate, hate, hate Donald Trump. If the election were over today, if just the early votes that have been cast so far were counted, Republicans would lose massively. It would not be close.”

He added, “We would lose both the House and the Senate. It would be a bloodbath.” 

Republican votes are “still out there” because they’re less likely to vote early, Cruz noted, and in Texas, there are still more registered Republicans than Democrats. Still, the current imbalance in voting data so far is “really, really big.”

Cruz then urged his listeners to vote for Republicans, either early or on Election Day.

“I want to ask you—I want to just about beg and plead—if you have not voted, if it’s still early voting in your state, come out and early vote,” he said. “If not, Election Day is Tuesday... Please, please, please, show up and vote.”

Among all states, Texas has seen the largest share of early voting at 36 percent, or 6.76 million ballots. Of them, 44 percent were cast by registered Democrats, 45 percent by Republicans, and 11 percent by another party.

“Texas is excruciatingly close,” Cruz said. “Understand, we could lose Texas. Let me repeat that: We could lose Texas—and by the way, not just the Senate race. We could lose every single statewide race in Texas. That’s how close these numbers are.”

A CNN/SSRS poll released Thursday for the Senate race between Democrat James Talarico and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton showed Talarico up six percent. In the same poll, Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa was down two percent.

“Now, some conservatives, they say, ‘I don’t trust the polls. The polls are all wrong.’ Well, let me tell you that there is a bias in the polls. They do skew left,” Cruz continued. “But I can tell you, having run a lot of campaigns, having examined a lot of numbers, these data are not fake. The Democrats are massively turning out the Republicans. We’ve got to fix that.”

Cruz went on to call the upcoming election “the most important midterm, I believe, of our lifetimes.”

Evan Vucci / REUTERSTed Cruz is warning that Republicans are staring down a midterm wipeout in Congress and across the state of Texas. 

Cruz said on his podcast he is “deeply, deeply worried” about the vote totals so far. As of Friday, four days out from Election Day, over 48 million mail-in and early in-person votes had been cast, with 47 percent being by registered Democrats and just 35 percent by Republicans.

The Texas senator has acknowledged that disdain for Trump is driving the GOP’s doomsday scenario.

news.title: Rubio welcomes Poland as G20 ‘full participant’, looks to Doral summit
news.text: Digital Desk | Atlanta, Oct 31 (IANS) US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has welcomed Poland as a “full participant” in the G20, saying President Donald Trump believes the country’s economic success and growing global influence are what the grouping needs, as foreign ministers met in Atlanta to prepare for the leaders’ summit at Doral. “I’d also like to take a moment to note the inclusion of Poland as a full participant in this G20,” Rubio said at the welcome reception for the G20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting at the Georgia Aquarium on Friday evening. “President Trump believes their economic success and growing global influence is exactly what the G20 needs to tackle the major economic challenges we all face, and we’re very excited to have them with us here today and this week,” he said. Earlier on Friday, Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski told reporters in Atlanta that India was among the countries he had lobbied to support Poland’s bid for permanent membership of the G20. “The United States has tabled a resolution to the effect that Poland would be a permanent member. And yes, I’ve been lobbying colleagues to support that motion, including India,” Sikorski said in response to a question from IANS. He noted that “the last, and if memory serves, only formal enlargement of the G20 happened under the Indian presidency,” which brought in the African Union, and said Prime Minister Narendra Modi, while receiving Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk in India a few days ago, had “committed India to supporting” Poland’s membership. Sikorski said he had asked all the ministers he met on the sidelines for support for Poland’s membership and that “almost all of them” agreed. “Some have already declared it publicly,” he said. In his remarks, Rubio said the ministers’ task was to prepare the ground for the summit of G20 leaders, hosted by the United States at Doral, Florida. “Our job is obviously, as I said earlier today, to create the platform in the – upon which our leaders will be able to meet in a few weeks in Doral and really have a successful G20,” he said. “This week we maintain that sharp focus on our economic interests, building on our prior meetings, and setting the stage for our leaders and their summit in Doral in just a few weeks,” Rubio said, adding that the US presidency had held gatherings on trade, fiscal and monetary policy, emerging technology and energy. He said it was “President Trump’s mission and many of your leaders’ missions to see that this group focuses on core economic policy issues.” “The economic challenges facing our countries are complex and they are interconnected. Because we all face these challenges, we must all work together to address them,” Rubio said. “The future of our nations depend on our willingness to understand that while our interests may not always align, we should always seek to work together to advance them when and where they do align,” he said. Rubio also said it was in the economic and national security interests of the United States “that we are energy dominant, that we have robust supply chains, that we remove the regulatory hurdles that hamper growth, and that we lead in the advancement of super intelligence and other critical emerging technologies.” The G20 foreign ministers conclude their meeting in Atlanta on Saturday with a session on supply chains and closing remarks by Rubio, according to the State Department’s public schedule.

news.title: Longtime Texas Republican Says GOP Has Become a 'Cult'
news.text: A former Republican congressman from Texas said the GOP is now a "cult organized around one man," arguing that President Donald Trump's influence has transformed the party and made him "a gift" to Democrats and other political opponents. Former Republican Congressman Alan Steelman said on CNN Friday that the party has steadily grown "darker and darker" since 2016. Steelman served as executive director of the Republican Party of Dallas County before being elected to Congress. He's among the Republicans crossing party lines to endorse Democrats. Steelman said he had long resisted describing the Republican Party as a cult but no longer believed the label could be avoided. "This grand old party [is] no longer grand, just old," Steelman said. "I've resisted for a long time using the word cult. But we're no longer a party, really. This is a cult organized around one man." Steelman, who represented Texas in Congress during the 1970s, said some supporters view former President Donald Trump as "a gift of God," before adding that Trump has instead become politically beneficial to his opponents. "Some of his supporters even refer to him as a gift of God, and I agree with that," Steelman said. "He's a gift, not to them. He's a gift to us." The former congressman framed his criticism as part of a broader attack on what he called changes in the Republican Party since Trump's rise to political prominence, arguing that the GOP had abandoned principles associated with Abraham Lincoln, Theodore Roosevelt and Dwight Eisenhower. Steelman, a Dallas businessman, is among a group of roughly 25 former Texas Republicans who have been campaigning for Democrat James Talarico in the Texas Senate race. Newsweek reached out to the National GOP for comment. Other Texas Republicans Endorsing Democrats Talarico’s campaign released a list of more than 20 Republicans endorsing him over his GOP opponent Ken Paxton. Some said their support was motivated largely by opposition to Paxton’s conduct during his time as Texas attorney general rather than a rejection of the Republican Party. The Republicans include former congressmen Steve Bartlett and Adam Kinzinger and Tom Phillips, the former chief justice of the Texas Supreme Court. Phillips wrote in an opinion piece that voters must decide which candidate "would best represent our state to the rest of the nation and the world." Paxton’s public career "has been marred almost since its inception by charges of impropriety, and his high-profile Senate race has exposed these controversies to tens of millions of Americans," Phillips wrote. "Paxton’s longstanding reputation will embarrass Texas in ways our state simply cannot afford." Phillips wrote that, while he does not agree with all of Talarico’s past statements or current positions, he is "confident that he would serve this great state with dignity and honor." Last week, Neil Bush, the brother of former President George W. Bush, revealed he had voted for Talarico, saying that character "matters more than party affiliation." What the Polls Show: Paxton v. Talarico CNN released a poll this week showing Talarico narrowly ahead with less than a week to go. ActiVote's newest survey of 400 likely voters, fielded October 22 to 28, had him up 52.1 percent to 47.9 percent, a lead that grew from 2 points a week earlier. Its margin of error was plus or minus 4.9 points. Texas Public Opinion Research had Talarico ahead 51 percent to 47 percent among 969 likely voters surveyed October 15 to 18, with a 3.9-point margin of error. His lead in that series has slipped by about a point a month since August, though he still carried independents 66 percent to 28 percent. A Fox News poll of 1,398 likely voters, taken October 15 to 19, found the race tied at 49 percent after Talarico led by 2 in September. Texas Southern University put the Democrat up 49 percent to 47 percent. The University of Houston's Hobby School of Public Affairs had Talarico at 48 percent and Paxton at 46 percent among 2,000 likely voters polled October 10 to 14, with Libertarian Ted Brown at 3 percent and a 2.9-point margin of error. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Former Republican Congressman Alan Steelman of Texas said the GOP is now a "cult organized around one man."
news.author: Jennifer Radcliffe

news.title: From fighting Covid to tackling cancer: Could mRNA vaccines transform medicine?
news.text:
The mRNA vaccines made global headlines when those developed by Pfizer and Moderna were the turning point in the fight against covid-19. That development followed years of little-known research which is now being boosted by millions of dollars or euros from investment funding.

Marco Cavaleri is the head of public health threats at the EMA and sees exciting potential in recent trials of mRNA in tackling other diseases.

“The biggest area that we are seeing really growing in numbers of candidates tested in clinical trials, is cancer. So the concept of personalised treatment of cancer is really high on the innovation agenda,” he said.

"And it’s not just cancer, it’s also cardiovascular disease, it’s also autoimmune diseases so really we could see a revolution in science and in medicine with this technology."

The idea behind personalised medicine is each patient gets a variation of the treatment based on the characteristics of their cancer or other illness.

Mr Cavaleri pointed to developments just this month in potential treatment for melanoma skin cancer when speaking to reporters at the EMA headquarters in Amsterdam.

Trials showed a personalised mRNA vaccine cut the chance of skin cancer returning or the patient dying by 42% when used with an immunotherapy medicine, the vaccine manufacturers MSD and Moderna said.

Mr Cavaleri described these findings as “a potential breakthrough for the future”.

He acknowledged it was early days, adding: "So it can happen also that we will see some failures but the road is paved towards exploring more in depth the ability of this technology for delivering products in a personalised way that would treat cancer." 

The mRNA technology could also be used, he added, in treatment with CAR-T therapy for blood cancers.

Hesitancy around vaccines

Ms Cooke also stressed “very impressive” innovations in the vaccine world but acknowledged the growing hesitancy around vaccines since the pandemic.

She took up the role of executive director in 2020, becoming the first woman to do so in the EMA’s quarter-century history, and she led the EU rollout of covid-19 vaccines.

Appointed initially for five years, her position was extended last year until her planned retirement next year.

She spoke of how, when her own now-adult children were young, she had them vaccinated against illnesses, including her daughter getting the HPV vaccine.

This offers protection against cervical cancer. Global evidence now is this vaccine is set to eliminate deaths from this devastating cancer.

“Vaccines are one of the most effective public health interventions that have ever been developed. They have saved lives and they continue to save lives,” Ms Cooke said.

In the area of childhood vaccines, she spoke of “some challenges” now to the uptake of measles vaccines.

In Ireland last year, the MMR vaccine uptake among children aged 24 months was only 86.3%. This is below the target of 95% needed to prevent outbreaks.

Ms Cooke told the Irish Examiner she would advise parents to ask questions if they are unsure about vaccination.

“I would advise you to go to trusted sources of information such as the European Medicines Agency. We really put a lot of effort into putting out fact-based information,” she said.

“We work with pediatricians, communications specialists. We try to ensure that the information we provide is unbiased, based on the science, independent and we try to put it in a way that’s easily understandable as well.” 

She said the EMA works with patient groups to make sure information addresses people’s everyday concerns.

“But honestly, I think the scientific figures showing the lives saved by vaccines are very impressive and I think people have just forgotten,” she said.

"And I’m just afraid people haven’t seen the diseases because vaccination has been so successful and that they can’t imagine a world where these diseases will come back. That’s one of the frightening things."

Before the measles vaccine was introduced in 1963 around the world, major epidemics broke out regularly, causing an estimated 2.6 million deaths every year, the World Health Organisation said.

“There’s been huge advances and we want that to continue, and that’s part of the message that I would like to share," Ms Cooke said.

She cautioned: “We now have children dying of diseases like measles or diphtheria, and we know the vaccines can provide protection. I think this is a challenge we really have to take on.” 

Speaking about choices, she said: “I don’t believe any parent sets out to do harm to their child by avoiding a vaccine. That’s not the reason, I think it’s all about getting the message right.” 

That messaging by the EMA about vaccines and medicines is becoming more visible globally as the American approach changes.

In just one example last month President Donald Trump proposed — without sharing any evidence for this — that vaccine makers split some childhood shots into five separate doses, which he believes will result in a reduction in autism rates, an idea repeatedly debunked by scientists.

Ms Cooke said the EMA worked very closely with the US FDA (Food and Drug Administration).

“One of the challenges for us is how we address sentiments that maybe are coming from the US system and how we ensure that we can provide the right information to counter anything that is either wrong or mis-informed,” she said.

“That is something that we really try to do.” 

A page on the EMA website titled “Vaccines: concerns, questions and false claims” answers common questions. 

“We either try to come out with something publicly or we develop lines to take for our network so [the national health authorities] have the fact-based information to counter some of the challenging assertions that may be coming from the US,” she said.

US a 'huge propagator' of global misinformation

The vaccine seminar also heard from Heidi Larson, professor of anthropology, risk and decision science at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine.

She described how multiple studies show vaccine hesitancy is growing, and in 2022 she was part of the latest analysis of the state of vaccine confidence in Europe.

“If you don’t understand what is behind it, we are never going to get it right in terms of how we engage and how we approach [people who are hesitant],” she said.

Part of this is understanding the influence of family, friends, religion and other non-medical sources of information, she added.

“It is again and again repeated that healthcare professionals are the most trusted. But who else are people trusting?” she said.

She also raised concerns about the role of America now in the health community, using an image of Robert F Kennedy Jnr, the US secretary of health.

She described the US as a “huge propagator” of global misinformation around vaccines.

“It’s really had a negative impact, and this was before the current administration, which has made things even more complicated in terms of policies coming out that totally contradict Europe and other countries; it confuses the public,” she said.

She said how, during the pandemic campaigns, questioning vaccines merged with other protest groups, adding: "They had the shared theme of against government control or freedom, liberty."

This has made it more challenging to discuss vaccine hesitancy, as people say their issue is not with any particular jab but about liberty.
news.summary: Emer Cooke highlights falling childhood vaccination rates as researchers explore personalised mRNA treatments for cancer and other diseases

news.title: US judge pushes back on Trump arch 'national security' argument
news.text: WASHINGTON, D.C. — A US federal judge on Friday pushed back on government assertions that President Donald Trump's planned massive arch in Washington is needed for national security.Trump did not mention national security concerns when first announcing plans to build the 250-foot (76-meter) triumphal white arch, which is modeled after the Arc de Triomphe in Paris.He said later, however, in a Truth Social post, that it would include a 'top grade military complex' that could house drones and snipers.District Judge Tanya Chutkan noted that the Republican president had also invoked national security in presenting the case for building a White House ballroom to the Supreme Court.'It doesn't make the use of national security talismanic in this case,' Chutkan said. 'This is the first time the government has proffered a national security aspect to this case.'Robert Stander, a Justice Department lawyer, said the arch is a 'high priority project' for the administration.The lawsuit being heard by Chutkan was brought by a group of Vietnam War veterans seeking to stop construction of the arch, which could begin as early as next week.Wendy Liu, a lawyer for the plaintiffs, said that given its massive size, the arch would obscure the sight lines between the Lincoln Memorial, one of Washington's iconic landmarks, and Arlington National Cemetery, the final resting place for hundreds of thousands of American servicemembers.The arch is one of a number of projects launched by Trump in a bid to put his personal stamp on the capital.They include the ballroom that is being built at the White House, for which Trump had an entire wing of the presidential mansion demolished.Another is the laborious renovation of the Reflecting Pool, a massive rectangular water basin on the National Mall.Trump has also proposed revamping the East Potomac Golf Links, a historic waterfront Washington golf course.That project is the focus of a bitter legal battle: the judge presiding over the case launched an investigation on Friday into whether lawyers for the Trump administration had lied to the court.For a time, Trump also had his name placed on the walls of the Kennedy Center, the culture and arts institute named after assassinated president John F. Kennedy, before a judge reversed the move.Chutkan did not make an immediate ruling in the arch case but said she would do so 'expeditiously.

news.title: Hannity Blindsided as His Own Callers Turn on Trump
news.text:
Fox News star Sean Hannity has been ambushed by fed-up Republicans who called into his radio show. 

Listeners ringed The Sean Hannity Show to raise concerns about President Donald Trump’s failure to deliver on his 2024 campaign promises that have the party in peril in the midterms, but Hannity remained defiant and defended the president.

“I think the disconnect here with everybody, I believe, is the frustration with the Republicans. And by no means is that an endorsement of the Democrats, but I also have a problem with thinking that I have to choose the lesser of two evils in that sense,” a man named Josh from Ohio said before being cut off by a defensive Hannity, according to a transcript from Media Matters for America.

Hannity fired back, “Is it really the lesser of two evils, or is this a battle between maybe some weak Republicans, I’ll concede the point, RINO Republicans, and those that would tread the Constitution, that agenda that I just read off, would that not forever destroy the country, the freedom, the liberty that we take—that we’ve had our entire lives?” 

The Ohio man was not swayed.

“I think the problem—why you have people that are hesitant to vote is because we were convinced by Donald Trump that he was different. And the results on the ground here for, you know, hardworking Americans working paycheck—” he continued before again being cut off. 

Hannity interjected, “You mean 3.5 percent GDP growth today, borders that are totally, completely closed, the largest tax cuts in history, the lowest murder rate in the history of the country. I mean, what are you—stopping Iran from ever having a nuclear weapon? Do you give him credit for anything?” 

When Josh then tried to talk about rising gas prices, Hannity again interjected, not wanting to hear anything negative about Trump.

Josh was not the only conservative fed up with MAGA. Travis from Virginia was very concerned about the war in Iran and unimpressed with Trump in his second term.

“I want to say I’ve been voting for Trump ever since he started this thing, but I’m kind of on the edge now with him because it’s just—it’s this childish act of his that he keeps, continues to do,” he told Hannity. “And, you know, both Democrats and Republicans alike, they can’t get their act together.” 

Hannity again tried to point to GDP growth, which does not cover the higher gas and grocery prices that have Americans hurting. As such, Travis pushed back. 

“We had no business going and fighting a war that we had nothing to use to fight with,” he said, highlighting the military’s reportedly depleted arsenal, which has been strained by the number of attempted drone strikes by Iran.

The pile-on was not over yet. A man named Jon called to say he was disillusioned with American politics and wasn’t going to vote at all this time. 

“I don’t feel like I need to go out and vote, and I don’t think I can vote for being represented anyway,” he said. “I don’t like any of these people.”

Hannity then argued with him for a moment, raising the specter of the Democratic Socialists of America, and concluded he understood he wouldn’t convince him to get out and vote.

news.title: Elon Musk Warns 2028 Democratic Sweep Could Mean ‘End of Democracy’
news.text: Billionaire Elon Musk issued a stark warning to voters if Democrats sweep the chambers of Congress and the presidency in 2028, saying it could lead to the "end of democracy." Musk's message comes just four days ahead of the midterm elections, where Democrats are favored to take the House and face a competitive battle to flip the Senate. In his post to X early Friday morning, Musk laid out his three concerns. The first, he says, Democrats will make Puerto Rico and the District of Columbia states, in an effort to achieve a strong majority in the Senate. Secondly, Musk warned that Democrats would open the borders and "legalize everyone living in America illegally to cement a permanent majority." Lastly, Musk said Democrats would increase the size of the Supreme Court in an effort to gain an immediate majority. "This would result in America becoming a permanent one-party state and the end of democracy in any meaningful sense of the word. All that is needed to ensure this doesn’t happen is 51 Republican senators in 2029. That is why you should vote for Republican senators this election. Other reasons are irrelevant compared to this one," Musk concluded in his post. Billionaire businessman Mark Cuban reacted to Musk's post on X saying: "I’m against all of these. The new force in politics and elections is independents. The fact independents are NOT an organized party, means we can individually do what we think is right, without regard to party politics. That is a force we have not seen before. And it is only growing as we all become increasingly disgusted by party politics. Pushing these would backfire on Democrats," Cuban said. This is not the first time the Tesla and SpaceX CEO has made a fourth quarter election warning. During the 2024 presidential election, Musk said that if President Donald Trump lost his race to then Vice President Kamala Harris, it would have been the last election for Americans due to immigration that would have turned the U.S. into a "single party country." Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during them. Trump's overall approval rating and ranking on specific policy issues like the economy, immigration, jobs and the ongoing war in Iran have recently slipped as households across America are consistently flagging affordability concerns. The polling lows come as Trump has crisscrossed the country in the lead-up to November 3, to rally for potentially vulnerable GOP candidates. Newsweek reached out to the White House, Musk via SpaceX, and the Democratic National Committee (DNC) by email on Friday for comment. What Democrats Have Said About Supreme Court Justices and Puerto Rico, D.C. Statehood Musk is not the first person to raise the concern of Democrats potentially expanding the Supreme Court or pushing D.C. and Puerto Rican statehood over the finish line. In April, Trump ripped into longtime political commentator James Carville over the thoughts, saying in part, "Wacko James Carville, a so-called Democrat 'strategist,' wants the Democrats to make D.C. and Puerto Rico States and, most importantly, pack the Supreme Court, putting 13 Justices on the Court. Other Dems want 21 Justices. If they pull off adding these two States, these Country Destroying Sleazebags will dominate politics in America, if we even have a Nation left, for 100 years (TERMINATE THE FILIBUSTER!)." House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries was asked if he supports adding more justices to the High Court earlier this year, and he responded saying that he supports reform. "What I support is dramatic reform, and what that looks like, to begin with, is making sure that the Supreme Court actually has an ethical code of conduct so that they’re not able to simply conduct themselves in ways that are inconsistent with the notion in this country that no one is above the law, " Jeffries said on NBC's Meet The Press in August. He added that Judiciary Committee Democrats will look further into what "dramatic reform" could be. Notably, Kamala Harris has previously supported the idea of adding justices to the Court and making D.C. and Puerto Rico states. “I believe that we need to expand the Supreme Court,” Harris said on the Baby, This is Keke Palmer podcast this month. “We need more justices on the Supreme Court so that we can have a court that actually reinforces the spirit and principles behind the Constitution of the United States.” She also supported pushing for Puerto Rico and D.C. statehood if their residents want it, during the podcast. Democratic Representative Jim Clyburn of South Carolina previously said he too would support adding seats to the High Court. Lawmakers recently voted on a GOP-backed amendment to cap the Supreme Court at nine justices. The vote failed to get two-thirds support. D. Stephen Voss, political professor at the University of Kentucky, told Newsweek on Friday in part, "Expanding the number of states in a way that would improve Democratic political fortunes has long been a goal among activists on the left, although it's unclear how broadly popular such proposals would be with mainstream Democratic politicians in Congress." Democrats and Immigration As Trump's second term is well underway, Democrats have made their opposition to his administration's immigration policies known. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids in major U.S. cities, deportations and fatal shootings involving federal agents have prompted Democrats to speak out in fury. Trump has made stricter border enforcement a key pillar of his presidency, including efforts to continue building a wall along the U.S.-Mexico border and initially suspending asylum at the border, which has faced legal setbacks. However, numerous Democrats, including candidates in key midterm races, have hit back at President Joe Biden's handling of the border, going as far as to say he "failed us." Democrats have also called for making the path to obtain U.S. citizenship simpler while leaning into ICE as a central focus of the midterms. Democratic candidates, like Florida's Angie Nixon and Minnesota's Peggy Flanagan, have called for ICE to be abolished or dismantled while advocating for a new immigration enforcement system to be built "from scratch." On its website, the DNC says in part that the party believes in "secure borders, common-sense immigration laws, and fair enforcement." "We also believe in the humanity and dignity of every person. Federal agents should not be able to take over your city, target children, or kill innocent people in the streets," the DNC added on its website. Voss later said in his response to Newsweek that, "On the other hand, the Democratic Party has not advocated either throwing open the borders or granting widespread amnesty to illegal migrants. At worst, a critic might argue that today's Democratic Party opposes most muscular policies intended to curtail immigration." How Much Money Has Musk Donated This Midterm Cycle? Earlier this month, The New York Times reported that Musk spent $276 million, with a majority going to the Senate Leadership Fund, this cycle. He also donated $76 million earlier this year to his America PAC, which has backed Republicans in House and Senate races. On Friday, The Times reported the total figure of Musk's spending has risen to nearly $475 million this cycle. Newsweek cannot independently verify that figure at the time of publication. Other outlets also highlight that Musk's spending has surpassed $400 million. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Samantha Beech and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Musk laid out his concerns if Democrats win the majority, while urging voters to back Republican senators in the midterms.

news.title: 'Shut up! Shut up, dope!' Trump loses it as three protesters interrupt him at rally
news.text:
President Donald Trump was thrice interrupted by protesters during his midterm rally in Florida, which visibly frustrated him.

The Daytona Beach stop is Trump's second Florida rally in a week, part of a red-state blitz in the final days before the midterms, CNN reported. Early in the speech, three different protesters interrupted his remarks, with each coming in short order.

When the third protester sounded off, Trump stopped mid-sentence while touting midterm enthusiasm, pointed and shouted, "Shut up! Shut up, dope!"

"These guys are losers, and it's always at my punchlines," Trump yelled. "I've had three unbelievable punchlines, and I've been hit three times at the punchline. They're going to go away thinking, 'Trump's a lousy speaker.' These guys are losers."

The crowd then chanted, "We love Trump!"

news.title: Russia uncompromising as Rubio hosts G20 talks in shadow of conflicts
news.text: ATLANTA, Georgia — Russia showed no sign Friday of softening its stance on Kyiv as G20 foreign ministers opened talks in the United States, with the Ukraine and Iran wars deepening rifts between the sprawling forum's members.Sharp disagreements emerged around the table, with EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas accusing Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov of presenting 'lies' on issues like the conflict in Ukraine.'He put forward a lot of lies, a lot of false narratives' that Europeans were able to push back on, Kallas told AFP.European officials also sought to put more pressure on Moscow, particularly to secure a ceasefire in the Black Sea, a key agriculture export corridor.Lavrov, in turn, was 'quite provocative' in his remarks, a European diplomatic source said.At a press conference, Lavrov criticized Europeans for their 'arrogant boycott' while praising the willingness of US President Donald Trump's administration to engage with Moscow.Plans for a traditional family photo of G20 ministers were called off as some European officials objected to appearing alongside Lavrov, a diplomatic source told AFP.European leaders have opted not to appear in photos with Russian delegations at other G20 meetings this year, as fighting drags on more than four years after Russia's invasion of Ukraine.A US official said the picture was cancelled to avoid allowing 'a ceremonial photo opportunity to become a diplomatic distraction.'The gathering in Atlanta, taking place just days before US midterm elections, sets the stage for a G20 leaders' summit at Trump's Doral resort in Miami in December.But it also comes as global energy prices have rocketed since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran in February. Tehran retaliated by choking off the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for oil and gas transit.Even as the United States seeks to focus on economic growth, trade imbalances and supply chain challenges — covering areas like energy and critical minerals — few breakthroughs are expected.Instead of a final declaration, the two days of talks are expected to conclude Saturday with a chair summary drafted by the United States.'Decent talk'Still, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told an opening plenary that the world faces a critical 'moment of choosing' as it grapples with 'interconnected economic and geopolitical crises.'He urged the Group of 20 forum -- which includes China, France, Germany, India, Japan and Russia -- to work together against threats like strains on global energy and food supply chains, and on freedom of navigation.Rubio spoke briefly with Lavrov on the sidelines of the G20 meeting, with the Russian minister saying both sides had a 'decent talk.'Moscow has been shunned by most of the West since it invaded Ukraine, and Lavrov himself remains under international sanctions.German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said that 'there is no normality with Russia,' and pledged to again 'call on Russia to finally accept Ukraine's offer of a ceasefire, starting in the Black Sea.'Rubio's interactions with Lavrov in Atlanta are being closely watched as Washington pursues diplomacy on Ukraine while seeking Moscow's cooperation on reining in fuel prices, a key campaign issue in US midterms.Lavrov's G20 appearance comes ahead of fresh negotiations expected between Moscow, Kyiv and Washington in November.Analysts say his presence is not surprising as Washington has welcomed Russian officials to this year's G20 events, while excluding member South Africa.Trump has invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to Florida in December as well and eased some sanctions on Moscow while touting a deal for Russia to sell diesel as prices soared, squeezing Americans.Another issue key to the US agenda is freedom of navigation.A US State Department official flagged 'shared resolve to confront urgent crises and keep critical sea lanes open to commerce without threats or tolls.'But the possibility of further escalation in the Middle East is mounting, with Trump signalling he could attack Iran after Tuesday's midterm elections.

news.title: Oil jumps 2pc
news.text:
HOUSTON: Oil prices jumped more than 2 percent on Friday and settled at their highest levels since the end of April, as traders braced for a potential escalation in the Iran war after the US midterm elections, with an attack on a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz highlighting supply risks.

Brent crude futures for December, which expired on Friday, settled up USD2.76, or 2.4 percent, at USD117.64 a barrel, after touching a high of USD118. The more active January contract gained USD2.63 to USD113.43.

US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures settled USD2.12, or 2.08 percent, higher at USD104.12.

For the month, Brent finished 13.6 percent higher, while WTI rose 15.2 percent.

“Traders will remain focused on oil flows out of the Middle East and the likely escalation by US and allied forces,” said Dennis Kissler, senior vice president of trading at BOK Financial.

On Friday, a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz was hit by explosive devices attached by a small boat, said the UKMTO, the British maritime security service. It was not immediately clear who was behind the attack in the strait, the key sea outlet for Gulf crude and fuel supplies.

It was the first known successful strike in the waterway using limpet mines, explosives that are attached to a ship’s hull from a small boat, since the US-Israeli war with Iran began in February, maritime sources said.

‘HIGHER LIKELIHOOD OF AN ESCALATION’

The US ordered non-emergency government employees and their family members to leave Saudi Arabia effective October 23 due to safety risks, the US embassy in Riyadh said on Friday, citing Houthi attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure.

Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi militants said on Thursday they had attacked several sites in Saudi Arabia, including the large Ras Tanura oil refinery, the Rabigh refinery and a production facility in Abqaiq owned by state oil company Saudi Aramco.

A Saudi-led coalition also said it had intercepted a cruise missile launched by the Houthis towards the kingdom’s western region.

Meanwhile, Qatari mediators returned to Tehran on Friday as part of coordinated efforts to reach a deal between the US and Iran, an official briefed on the talks told Reuters.

US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that Vice President JD Vance had reached out to Iran to help the country get medical supplies, after US media reported Vance had written to Tehran’s top security official to revive peace talks.

Iran has received a letter from Vance, but it has not responded to it yet, Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency reported, adding that Tehran wants the US to meet its conditions and “any position that contradicts this framework is unacceptable.”

Oil prices could become even more volatile in the next couple of weeks due to Israel’s recent elections and the US midterm elections on November 3, according to a Saxo Bank briefing on Thursday.

The Danish bank said crude is expected to trade in a higher range of USD70 to USD90 a barrel even after the conflict ends, compared with a pre-war range of USD60 to USD70.

Saudi exports rise

Saudi Arabia’s crude exports rose in October from September, two of three ship-tracking companies said, despite Iranian attacks on shipping in the Gulf and claims by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis of attacks on Saudi oil facilities.

The US oil rig count, an indicator of future output, rose by two. US crude oil output increased in August, while demand for crude oil and petroleum products declined, the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) said in its Petroleum Supply Monthly report on Friday.

Meanwhile, Libya’s National Oil Corporation said an armed group shut a valve on Friday on the main Hamada crude oil pipeline, which links the Hamada field to the Zawiya refinery. It said the closure of the valve had halted the flow of about 15,000 barrels per day.

news.title: Rifts over wars in Ukraine, ME loom over G20 meeting
news.text:
ATLANTA: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged fellow G20 foreign ministers on Friday to work together for greater geopolitical stability and economic prosperity, warning that a series of crises posed serious threats to the global economic order.

But Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov’s participation in the two-day gathering in Atlanta has roiled many G20 ministers, aggravating deep rifts over the wars in Ukraine and the Middle Eastthat experts and diplomats say could thwart real progress at the meeting.

Canada’s foreign minister, Anita Anand, who has been critical of Lavrov’s participation, missed the opening plenary session.

Her spokeswoman said she was arriving late from a Canada-EU summit in Montreal.

South Africa’s minister was also absent, not invited by the US, which holds this year’s rotating presidency.

A traditional G20 family photo was left off Rubio’s official schedule after some European officials said they would not be photographed with Lavrov. A third of the participants objected, including Australia and Canada, a Western diplomat said.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul told reporters that he expected the family photo to be scrapped entirely, adding, “In no case will there be a family photo with European partners and Mr. Lavrov together because, as I said yesterday, there is no normalcy with Russia.”

The US has sought to focus its allies on trade imbalances while building a coalition to counter China’s control of critical minerals, but the wars and their economic impact remain the top concern for many G20 members.

In his opening remarks, Rubio said the world faced various crises that threatened global energy and food supply, trade, and the freedom of navigation.

“We are tasked, on behalf of the nations that we serve, to work together with one another to coordinate responses to emerging crises and to protect our shared interests,” he said. “We can help set the context for expanded geopolitical stability and the broader economic prosperity agenda that our leaders will tackle.”

With G20 members Russia, China and middle powers such as Brazil and India trying to navigate US-China strategic competition, you have “much more of a split than we’ve ever had,” said Heidi Crebo-Rediker, who was chief economist at the State Department during the Obama administration.

Over the past decade or so, G7 countries would at least “have agreed a coordinated platform before they came to the G20, but now we don’t even really have that,” she added.

A State Department official told reporters that four G20 ministerial-level meetings held this year had achieved some consensus, but more work was needed before the December 14 to 16 leaders’ summit in Miami.

Rubio has championed the Pax Silica initiative, aimed at uniting G20 countries concerned about China’s dominance in rare earths and other critical minerals.

But any movement on that front will probably come afterwards, experts said, pointing to a US-led statement on excess industrial capacity that some G20 trade ministers signed after the group failed to reach consensus.

Elaine Dezenski of the Washington-based Foundation for Defense of Democracies said such statements by ad hoc groups could offer a

way forward in the current environment.

“The right test is whether the US can build cooperation with partners when all-member consensus appears to be out of reach,” she said. She noted the Quad — a security grouping of the US, India, Japan and Australia — would also meet in Atlanta in coming days.

Disagreement Over US Actions Toward Russia

US President Donald Trump’s recent decisions on Russia, including a deal to buy diesel and waiving some sanctions, could also weigh on discussions, along with Ukraine’s problems with its Starshield satellite services.

“If it’s not brought up, it’s certainly the elephant in the room that the US — and Trump in particular — has taken a very solid stance together with (Russian President) Vladimir Putin and against Ukraine,” Crebo-Rediker said.

European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said she would call for increased support for Ukraine, while pushing for progress on accountability measures through the Special Tribunal and Claims Commission.

“Russia must be accountable,” she wrote on X.

Some countries may seek to avoid conflict, including Canada, Mexico, India and others still negotiating trade agreements with the US, said one G20 diplomat who declined to be named. “Everyone is trying to keep a low profile.”

The meetings take place a day after Commerce Department data showed the US economy grew at its fastest pace in a year in the third quarter, buoyed by AI investment, even as other countries face slower growth or even contractions.

They also fall just days before the November 3 midterm elections, which polls indicate could leave Trump without majorities in either house of Congress.

Although Ukraine has not been invited to join the G20 ministers in Atlanta, Trump is also pushing hard for a ceasefire in Russia’s war in Ukraine. Russia, Ukraine and the US are expected to hold technical-level trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi next month.

news.title: Halloween Protests & French Promises, US Mid Term Mood, What now for Israel?
news.text:
In Israel, an inconclusive election has left both Benjamin Netanyahu and his rival Gadi Eisenkot claiming victory, with neither securing the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority. Arab parties have made historic gains, potentially holding the balance of power, but Netanyahu is challenging the legitimacy of their result, while Eisenkot insists on a Zionist government.

Meanwhile, in the US, the final days of the midterm campaign have taken a distinctly theatrical turn, as Donald Trump and Barack Obama trade barbs in a public back-and-forth involving gold-plated White House décor, accusations of elitism and an unlikely cameo from the Cheesecake Factory.

news.summary: France braces for another weekend of unrest as the Yellow Vests return to the streets under the rallying cry of ‘Act III – Halloween’, with 70,000 police and security forces deployed after the riots and looting of recent weeks. A cash-strapped government faces mounting grievances, a rolling protest movement and little room for manoeuvre ahead of elections, as it struggles to restore order while grappling with crippling debt.

news.title: 'The View' co-hosts agree Democrats should not impeach Trump if party wins back control of Congress
news.text: "The View" co-hosts agreed with former Vice President Kamala Harris Friday that impeachment would not be a good use of the Democratic Party’s time and resources if the party wins back control of Congress in the midterm elections. "I think that going on in the direction of impeachment is not a good idea," Harris warned Tuesday on "The Parnas Perspective" podcast. "OK, just to be honest with you. Because we have limited resources, and I think the energy and the resources need to be put into accountability, need to be put into investigations. And that's where the time should be spent. Remember, I was in the Senate for the last go-round and the votes aren't there, right? So, that's how I feel." After playing a clip of Harris' comments, "The View" co-hosts agreed with her assessment. KAMALA HARRIS BREAKS WITH LEFT FLANK, WARNS DEMS THAT IMPEACHING TRUMP IS 'NOT A GOOD IDEA' "In terms of Trump, no, I don't think that's what should be on the agenda," co-host Sunny Hostin said. "Hakeem Jeffries — who I believe will be the next speaker of the House, after November — he has a plan for 100 days which includes tax credits, taking care of the tax credits, limiting ICE and also stock trades. "And then he's got a plan for the first 100 hours, which would include, you know, just undoing a lot of unpopular Trump policies. So, I think there is a plan in place that Democrats have, and it may not include impeaching Trump." "I think that Democrats have to be realistic of what's achievable," co-host Ana Navarro said. "We are four days away from the election. So, before we start talking about what Democrats are going to do once they win, they've got to make sure they win. "People have to focus not on all of the conversation about impeachment and what is going to happen but rather on getting out the vote and getting people to the polls so that the American people decide who they want in power in the House and in the Senate. "There's a limit to what Democrats are going to be able to do even if they win the House, even if they win the House and the Senate, because Donald Trump is still president," she continued. "Legislation in this country needs to be signed by the president. If not, it needs to have a veto-proof majority. And I think that's going to be very difficult to achieve. I'm completely against impeachment. "There's 100 other ways to hold Donald Trump and his administration accountable," Navarro added. "Impeachment is an exercise that's moot if you don't have the 67 votes in the Senate required to indict." news.title: Santa Monica Gallery Turns Decorated Lunch Bags Into Art for One Night Only
news.text:
At Craig Krull Gallery in Bergamot Station Arts Center, decorated paper lunch bags will move from meal service to exhibition walls for one evening. Westside H.O.D.G. will host its Lunch Bag Art Exhibition from 4 to 6 p.m. Nov. 1. The bags are made by volunteers for a Sunday meal effort that has operated across Los Angeles since 2020.

Organizers told the Santa Monica Daily Press that the Sunday Lunch Bag Project has reached nearly 1 million hungry people since it began during the pandemic in 2020. Volunteers decorate the bags before filling them with meals for distribution. Donations at the exhibition will support the project, Westside H.O.D.G. and student clubs at Santa Monica and Culver City high schools.

A Project Born Out of 2016 Living Rooms

The roots of the project trace back to Hancock Park, where Jennifer Levin founded H.O.D.G. — short for Hang Out Do Good — in 2016. Levin and friends began gathering in one another's homes after Donald Trump's election that year to talk about becoming better citizens, according to the same report, and the group's early efforts included petitions, postcard writing, protests, door knocking, and food and clothing drives. Levin has said she had long wanted an adult group that resembled Boy or Girl Scouts, where members learn skills and do good deeds together.

The lunch-bag collaboration itself pairs H.O.D.G. with the Hollywood Food Coalition, known as HoFoCo, which describes the partnership as a joyful collaboration distributing bags directly to individuals and families experiencing homelessness and food insecurity throughout Los Angeles County. A typical bag includes a hearty sandwich — nut butter and jelly, turkey, or ham — along with fruit or a healthy fruit pouch, per HoFoCo's own description of the program. HoFoCo delivers the volunteer-made lunches to more than 20 partner nonprofits, including Food on Foot, The People Concern and Covenant House, the Daily Press reports.

Why Sundays Became the Group's Mission

Levin has said HoFoCo specifically requested Sunday deliveries because most organizations feeding unhoused people are closed that day. Westside H.O.D.G. launched in May 2025 when Alison Rou and Loren Segan started the chapter, with state Senator Ben Allen attending the group's first meeting as a guest, according to the Daily Press. The Westside chapter initially offered 100 lunches to the Hollywood Food Coalition but delivered 400 on its first Sunday, and organizers say it has not missed a Sunday delivery since.

The larger collaboration has also maintained a weekly schedule, according to the Daily Press, which quoted an organizer: “We've never missed a Sunday. Not for Christmas, not for the LA Marathon.” Segan has described the decorated bags as messages of hope and reminders to recipients that they are not alone. Levin has said she considers the bags art because of the emotional response they can inspire.

Student Clubs Behind the Decorated Bags

High school involvement has become a backbone of the Westside effort. Kaeli founded the club at Santa Monica High School and Olivia founded the one at Culver City High School, with both having made project lunches alongside their families since middle school, the Daily Press reports. Their clubs rely on bake sales and donations to fund gatherings that can turn out anywhere from 40 to 150 lunches at a time.

Olivia recalled a Sunday when she realized the bags her group had made would feed 150 people that day, according to the Daily Press. Bonnie Friedericy, a Hollywood Food Coalition volunteer, is among those who help with the broader distribution effort.

Gallery Space Donated Between Shows

The exhibition landed at Craig Krull Gallery after Krull offered the space between two other shows, the Daily Press reports. Krull had previously organized Out of the Ashes at Bergamot Station, an exhibition for artists who lost homes and studios in the Palisades and Eaton fires, making the lunch bag show something of a continuation of his gallery's recent focus on community response. The one-night exhibition will include work by both well-known working artists and everyday volunteers who have decorated bags for the project.

Food access and getting to the gallery

The project’s focus on meal access sits within a wider county need: the LA County Department of Homeless Services and Housing says more than 1.3 million people in the county rely on food assistance programs. That figure describes overall reliance on food assistance; it does not establish how many people lack access to meals on Sundays. Craig Krull Gallery says its earlier Out of the Ashes exhibition ran from February 19 to March 1, began as a fire-relief effort and gave artists a venue to share responses to the fires—a different purpose from the lunch-bag project’s recurring meal distributions. For visitors traveling to the exhibition, the Bergamot Station Arts Center visitor guide lists the Metro Expo E Line’s 26th Street Bergamot stop as a transit option.

Meal-count figures tied to the broader Sunday Lunch Bags collaboration vary depending on the source: HangOutDoGood's own materials have cited almost 900,000 lunches delivered to partner organizations over six years, while HoFoCo's press materials describe close to 700,000 meals provided, and a separate report put the figure at 690,000 meals distributed. The Daily Press's nearly 1 million figure reflects organizers' own account of the project's reach since 2020.

Alison Rou has urged Westside residents to subscribe to the chapter's newsletter and join the lunch makers directly. Those interested in getting involved can reach the group at hodgwestla@gmail.com or through hangoutdogood.com/westside-la.
news.summary: Westside H.O.D.G. hosts a one-night Lunch Bag Art Exhibition Nov. 1 at Craig Krull Gallery, backing a project that has fed Angelenos since 2020.

ATLANTA - Japan called on Russia to immediately release a detained Japanese journalist in a meeting between their foreign ministers, the Japanese Foreign Ministry said.

Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi made the call as he met his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov on the sidelines of a Group of 20 foreign ministers meeting in the U.S. state of Georgia.

G20 foreign ministers meet amid high oil prices, wars in Iran and Ukraine

ATLANTA - Foreign ministers from the Group of 20 major economies met Friday to discuss geopolitical tensions, energy security and strengthening supply chains as the world remains rocked by high oil prices and the wars in Iran and Ukraine.

The two-day meeting, held in the southern U.S. state of Georgia and hosted by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, sets the stage for the G20 summit in Florida in December to be chaired by President Donald Trump.

TOKYO - The Japanese government is unlikely to label China as a "threat" in its key security strategy document to be revised by the year-end, possibly retaining the current language that describes Beijing's assertiveness as "the greatest strategic challenge," sources close to the matter said Friday.

The idea to not use tougher language against China is apparently to avoid fueling further tensions to already strained Sino-Japanese ties, at a time when the United States, Japan's close security ally, has been moving to build a "constructive relationship of strategic stability" with the world's second-largest economy.

TOKYO - The Bank of Japan on Friday said underlying inflation had "generally" reached its 2 percent target after a nearly 14-year effort involving unconventional monetary easing, with its governor signaling room for further interest rate hikes to stabilize prices over the longer term.

After the BOJ decided to leave its policy rate steady at 1.25 percent as widely expected, Governor Kazuo Ueda stressed that the central bank's policy focus has shifted toward containing inflation and anchoring it at its 2 percent target, a departure from years of efforts to push up prices.

Japan Foreign Ministry hit by hacking, along with ANA, Muji brand operator

TOKYO - The Japanese Foreign Ministry said Friday its network connected to external systems has been targeted by unauthorized access, leading to a possible personal information leak, while more major companies from various sectors reported potential or actual breaches.

According to the Foreign Ministry, about 3,600 records containing personal information, such as email addresses and names, may have been compromised, including 900 records belonging to people outside the ministry.

news.title: Trump praises Russia’s actions in Hubbard’s release
news.text:
WASHINGTON, October 31. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump praised Russia’s actions in connection with the release of American citizen Stephen Hubbard, who was convicted in Russia of taking part in hostilities on the side of Ukrainian forces.

"And so, as you know, he was somebody I wanted to get back, and I spoke to [Russian] President [Vladimir] Putin, and they said we'll let him come back," Trump told reporters on Friday during a meeting with Hubbard at the White House. "It was really an honor to help. It was just a spur of the moment. I said, ‘Do me a favor. Will you let Stephen Hubbard out? Let him out.’ And they were very nice in that regard," the US leader stressed.

Hubbard was convicted of taking part in hostilities on the side of Ukrainian forces. On October 7, 2024, the Moscow City Court sentenced him to six years and 10 months in a general-regime penal colony. Hubbard pleaded guilty to the charges. The time he spent in pretrial detention since April 2022 was credited toward his sentence.

The American’s release was announced during US Special Presidential Envoy Steve Witkoff’s visit to St. Petersburg. Russian Presidential Press Secretary Dmitry Peskov told TASS that Putin had decided to release Hubbard as a gesture of goodwill.

news.title: Why Trump’s Rallies Are Turning Into Epic Disasters: Journos
news.text:
Donald Trump is growing frustrated that his rallies are not the draw they used to be—all while hecklers make themselves heard like never before. 

Trump has suffered a string of embarrassments on the rally stage on the home stretch of the midterm campaign season, which Daily Beast Executive Editor Hugh Dougherty believes led to his eyebrow-raising—but short-lived—cancellation of rallies in must-win states for his party.

Trump, 80, has faced a barrage of hecklers nationwide this month. In Kansas, they interrupted his speech six times. In Ohio, the president had his mandatory thirsting of Sen. Jon Husted’s body interrupted by a protester who reminded everyone: “Trump went on the Jeffrey Epstein plane!” 

In Mississippi, a heckler told Trump to “shove that ballroom up your fat a--!”

Trump’s rallies “are being flooded with protests, and these protests have now become the thing that everybody is talking about,” Dougherty said. Host Joanna Coles said the heckling has been “hilarious.”

Dougherty believes the embarrassing moments are getting to the image-obsessed president.

Not only has heckling derailed Trump’s rallies, but clips of opponents being interviewed have also gained traction. One attendee of a South Carolina rally flustered a Fox News reporter by comparing the scene to the Jonestown mass murder-suicide cult.

“This is what people are seeing on television,” Dougherty said. “This is what people are seeing on social media. Not just people who hate Trump are seeing this. That’s what people in the Trump world are seeing as well. They are seeing these rallies go not well. They’re seeing them.”

Protesters are getting more attention, Dougherty added, because fewer Trump supporters are showing up.

“The venues are getting smaller. The seats are getting emptier,” he said. “It’s not the balm to Trump’s ego that it had been.”

At a San Antonio rally on Oct. 8, for instance, Trump boasted that he had filled the arena—only for a C-SPAN camera to show dozens of empty seats in the upper section moments later.

The week prior, the president’s visit to deep-red Mobile, Alabama, saw empty row upon empty row in the upper deck. Local media reported that the arena, built for around 10,000 people, had around 8,000 rallygoers.

The empty seats becoming a story has irked Trump, who has resorted to explaining why he believes the lack of people showing up to see him is actually not what it seems.

“There are no empty seats, there haven’t been for years, and there never will be,” he fumed on Truth Social after the lackluster turnout in Mobile. “The Rallies are ‘HOTTER’ than ever. They are all ‘happenings,’ and they never happened before, and will never be duplicated again. The Networks refuse, however, under any circumstances, to show the Crowds, but you can hear the thunderous applause, and know that it represents thousands and thousands of people.”

news.title: Trump rallygoers treating red state stops like ‘farewell tour’: MAGA expert
news.text:
President Donald Trump’s red-state rallies have become a chance for some supporters to see him “play the hits" one more time, according to The Good Liars’ Jason Selvig.

“In a weird way, this feels like a farewell tour,” Selvig told Molly Jong-Fast on her “Fast Politics” podcast, describing conversations with attendees in South Carolina and Georgia. 

“Some people are going there, treating it like a farewell tour,” he said Friday. “People have said, like, ‘I just never saw him before, and I want to go. I’m gonna go to a rally and see him and hear him play the hits.’”

Selvig said the crowds were large and enthusiastic, with supporters eager to hear Trump deliver his familiar one-liners. One woman attending her fifth rally told him she enjoyed watching newcomers experience the president's dancing and riffing with the crowd.

Jong-Fast compared the MAGA spectacle to a Grateful Dead concert.

“It’s an experience that you get to have in like a community there,” Selvig said.

But that enthusiasm did not always translate into interest in the election. Selvig recalled encountering people in Nebraska who seemed unaware that the midterms were happening.

“I don't think a lot of them care about the midterms,” he told the podcast host Friday. “It’s more about Trump’s star power, and they still love Trump.”

He stressed that other attendees were committed Republicans supporting local candidates, and that the rallies could motivate turnout.

Still, some supporters described the events primarily as entertainment.

“We heard that like three times in South Carolina — not a political rally — it's a show,” Selvig said.
